metadata.title: Crossed simplicial groups and structured surfaces

extraction_notes.note: Example environments that in fact define the planar crossed simplicial groups (cyclic, dihedral, paracyclic, ...); kept as example (illustrating crossed simplicial group) rather than retyped to definition, but used as definitions downstream.
Custom 'Reformulation' environment typed as remark; it restates Example 2.33(2) algebro-geometrically and quotes a cited result.
Proof has text ('Parts (a), (b1-2) are obvious.') before its single label 'Part (c)'; the immediate-sentence rule would merge everything into one step, so the proof gets zero steps.

Twisted-nerve constructions for the quaternionic, N-dihedral and N-quaternionic cases (Sec. 1.6.2) and the Lambda-, Xi- and nabla-trace descriptions (Sec. 1.7.3) are left inside running text; only the cyclic/twisted cyclic nerve and the paracyclic trace are nodes.
Tables 1-3 (types of invariants, the 7 crossed simplicial group types, planar correspondence) and the Galois-type diagram of planar Lie groups carry content only as tables; not represented as nodes.
The proof of Theorem A.9 is prose containing Lemma A.10 and its proof; the final sentence 'This proves the lemma and Theorem A.9' closes both, so both proof nodes end there.

nodes.statement: For a more analytic point of view, consider the subgroup of conformal linear transformations \[ Conf(2) \,\,=\,\, (Z/2)ltimes C^* \,\,subset \,\, GL(2,R) \] which is homotopy equivalent to GL(2,R), so that connective coverings of the two groups are in bijection. Denoting by G_conf the preimage of Conf(2) in G, we can consider surfaces with G_conf-structure which are essentially algebro-geometric objects: if G preserves orientation, we obtain Riemann surfaces, otherwise Klein surfaces . Such objects have moduli spaces M^G (more precisely, stacks) which are algebro-geometric counterparts of the groups Mod^G(S).
nodes.raw_latex:
For a more analytic point of view, consider the subgroup of conformal linear transformations
\[
\operatorname{Conf}(2) \,\,=\,\, (\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes \mathbb{C}^* \,\,\subset \,\, GL(2,\mathbb{R})
\]
which is homotopy equivalent to $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$, so that connective coverings of the two groups are in bijection.
Denoting by $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$ the preimage of $\operatorname{Conf}(2)$ in $\mathbb{G}$, we can consider surfaces with
$G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure which are essentially algebro-geometric objects: if $\mathbb{G}$
preserves orientation, we obtain Riemann surfaces, otherwise Klein surfaces \cite{alling-greenleaf}.
Such objects have moduli spaces $\mathcal{M}^G$ (more precisely, stacks) which are algebro-geometric
counterparts of the groups $\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S)$.

nodes.name: crossed simplicial group
nodes.statement: A crossed simplicial group is a category Delta G equipped with an embedding i:Delta to Delta G such that: item the functor i is bijective on objects, item any morphism u: i[m] to i[n] in Delta G can be uniquely expressed as a composition i(phi) circ g where phi: [m] to [n] is a morphism in Delta and g is an automorphism of i[m] in Delta G.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defi:csg} A {\em crossed simplicial group} is a category $\Delta \mathfrak{G}$ equipped with an embedding
	$i:\Delta \to \Delta \mathfrak{G}$ such that:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item the functor $i$ is bijective on objects,
		\item any morphism $u: i[m] \to i[n]$ in $\Delta \mathfrak{G}$ can be uniquely expressed as 
			a composition $i(\phi) \circ g$ where $\phi: [m] \to [n]$ is a morphism in
			$\Delta$ and $g$ is an automorphism of $i[m]$ in $\Delta \mathfrak{G}$.
	\end{enumerate}
nodes.clean_text: A crossed simplicial group is a category Delta G equipped with an embedding i:Delta to Delta G such that: item the functor i is bijective on objects, item any morphism u: i[m] to i[n] in Delta G can be uniquely expressed as a composition i(phi) circ g where phi: [m] to [n] is a morphism in Delta and g is an automorphism of i[m] in Delta G.
nodes.label: defi:csg

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{prop:skeleton}
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
		\item For every morphism $\phi: [m] \to [n]$ in $\Delta$, the association
		$g\mapsto \phi^* g$ defines a
		 map of sets
			\[
				\phi^*: \mathfrak{G}_n \longrightarrow \mathfrak{G}_m,\; g \mapsto \phi^*g
			\]
		The association $\phi \mapsto \phi^*$ makes the family $\mathfrak{G}=(\mathfrak{G}_n)_{n\geq 0}$ 
		into a simplicial set. The maps $\phi^*$ preserve unit elements but not necessarily the group structure.

		\item For objects $[m],[n]$, the association
			\[
				(\phi,g) \mapsto g^*\phi
			\]
			determines a right action of $\mathfrak{G}_n$ on the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([m],[n])$. 
			In the case $m=n$, this action preserves the identity morphism.

		\item In addition, we have the identities
			\begin{align*}
			\phi^*(g \circ h) & = \phi^*g \circ (g^*\phi)^*h,\\
			g^*(\phi \circ \psi) & = g^*\phi \circ (\phi^*g)^*\psi.
			\end{align*}
			
			\item Conversely, any sequence of groups $\mathfrak{G}=(\mathfrak{G}_n)$
	with operations
	\[
	(\phi,g) \mapsto (\phi^*(g),g^*(\phi))
	\]
	satisfying the compatibilities  (a) - (c),  uniquely determines a
	crossed simplicial group.  

			
	\end{enumerate}

group.

nodes.statement: Let us point out the following special cases of canonical factorization in a crossed simplicial group Delta G: \[ Hom_Delta G([n], [0]) cong G_n, Hom_Delta G([0], [n]) cong \0,1,dots, n\ times G_0. \] The first identification follows from the fact that Hom_Delta([n], [0]) = ptnolimits. Note that the simplicial set structure on \G_n\ can be deduced immediately from this identification: Hom_Delta G(-, [0]) is a contravariant functor on Delta G and, by restriction, on Delta. The second identification follows from the canonical identification of Hom_Delta([0], [n]) with \0,1,cdots, n\ given by evaluation.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:extreme} 
Let us point out the following special cases of canonical factorization in a crossed simplicial
group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$:
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([n], [0]) \cong \mathfrak{G}_n, \quad \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n]) \cong \{0,1,\dots, n\} \times \mathfrak{G}_0. 
\]
The first identification follows from the fact that $\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([n], [0]) = \operatorname{pt}\nolimits$. Note that the
simplicial set structure on $\{\mathfrak{G}_n\}$ can be deduced immediately from this identification:
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(-, [0])$ is a contravariant functor on ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ and, by restriction, on $\Delta$. 
The second identification follows from the canonical identification of $\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n])$ with
$\{0,1,\cdots, n\}$ given by evaluation.

\[
	\lambda: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\mathcal Set}, \; [n] \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([0], [n])/\mathfrak{G}_0
\]
where $\lambda([n])$ can be canonically identified with the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([0],[n]) \cong \{0,1,\dots,n\}$.

\[
	\lambda_{n}: \mathfrak{G}_n \longrightarrow S_{n+1}.
\]

\label{thm:classification} Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a crossed simplicial group.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item There is a canonical functor $\pi: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \to {\Delta {\mathfrak W}}$.
	\item For every $n \ge 0$, we have an induced short exact sequence of groups
		\[
			1 \longrightarrow \mathfrak{G}_n' \longrightarrow \mathfrak{G}_n \longrightarrow \mathfrak{G}_n'' \longrightarrow 1
		\]
	      where $\mathfrak{G}_n'$ and $\mathfrak{G}_n''$ denote kernel and image, respectively, of the induced
	      homomorphism $\pi_n: \mathfrak{G}_n \to W_{n+1}$. The short exact sequences assemble to a
	      sequence of functors
	      \[
			{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}' \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}'' 
	      \]
	      where ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}'$ is a simplicial group (Example \ref{exa:deviation}) and ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}'' \subset {\Delta {\mathfrak W}}$ is a crossed
	      simplicial subgroup of ${\Delta {\mathfrak W}}$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Consider the functor \[ lambda: Delta G longrightarrow mathcal Set, \; [n] mapsto Hom_Delta G([0], [n])/G_0 \] from Proposition . We claim that lambda admits a canonical factorization over the forgetful functor Delta mathfrak W to mathcal Set. Note that, via lambda, the group G_n acts canonically on the set Hom_Delta([0],[n]) = \0,1,dots,n\ of vertices of the combinatorial n-simplex. A vertex i in \0,1,dots,n\ can be canonically identified with the corresponding degeneracy map \[ s_i: [n+1] longrightarrow [n],\; j mapsto j & for j le i,\\ j-1 & for j > i. \] Explicitly, given g in G_n and i in \0,1,dots,n\, we have a commutative square \[ xymatrix [n+1] ar[d]_s_j^*g ar[r]^s_i & [n] ar[d]^g\\ [n+1] ar[r]^s_j & [n] \] where j = lambda(g)(i). Clearly, the map lambda(s_j^*g) induces a map from the fiber s_i^-1(i) = \i,i+1\ to the fiber s_j^-1(j) = \j,j+1\ which is either order preserving or order reversing. Therefore, we can lift lambda(g) in S_n+1 to a signed permutation \[ widetildelambda(g) = (varepsilon_0, varepsilon_1, dots, varepsilon_n ; lambda(g)) in Z/2Z wreath S_n+1 \] where \[ varepsilon_i = 0 & if lambda(s_j^*g): \i,i+1\ to \j,j+1\ is order preserving,\\ 1 & if lambda(s_j^*g): \i,i+1\ to \j,j+1\ is order reversing. \] Using the unique factorization property in Delta G, it is straightforward to verify that the association g mapsto widetildelambda(g) extends to provide a functor \[ widetildelambda: Delta G longrightarrow Delta mathfrak W \] commuting with the forgetful functors to mathcal Set, which proves (1). The remaining statements are easy to verify, the only nonobvious point being that Delta G' is in fact noncrossed simplicial. But this follows from the construction of widetildelambda: For g in G_n, the condition lambda(g) = id in S_n+1 implies that g^* fixes all face maps [n-1] to [n]. The condition that all signs varepsilon_i of the lift widetildelambda(g) are 0 implies that g^* fixes all degeneracy maps [n+1] to [n]. But this implies that Delta G'' is a simplicial group (cf. Example ).

Consider the functor
		\[
			\lambda: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\mathcal Set}, \; [n] \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([0], [n])/\mathfrak{G}_0
		\]
	from Proposition \ref{prop:forget}. 
	We claim that $\lambda$ admits a canonical factorization over the forgetful functor ${\Delta {\mathfrak W}} \to {\mathcal Set}$. 
	Note that, via $\lambda$, the group $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts canonically on the set
	$\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([0],[n]) = \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ of vertices of the combinatorial $n$-simplex. 
	A vertex $i \in \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ can be canonically identified with the corresponding degeneracy map
	\[
		s_i: [n+1] \longrightarrow [n],\; j \mapsto \begin{cases} j & \text{for $j \le i$,}\\
			j-1 & \text{for $j > i$.} \end{cases}
	\] 
	Explicitly, given $g \in \mathfrak{G}_n$ and $i \in \{0,1,\dots,n\}$, we have a commutative square
	\[
		\xymatrix{
			[n+1] \ar[d]_{s_j^*g} \ar[r]^{s_i} & [n] \ar[d]^g\\
			[n+1] \ar[r]^{s_j} & [n]
		}
	\]
	where $j = \lambda(g)(i)$. Clearly, the map $\lambda(s_j^*g)$ induces a map from the fiber
	$s_i^{-1}(i) = \{i,i+1\}$ to the fiber $s_j^{-1}(j) = \{j,j+1\}$ which is either order
	preserving or order reversing. Therefore, we can lift $\lambda(g) \in S_{n+1}$ to a signed permutation 
	\[
		\widetilde{\lambda}(g) = (\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n ;
		\lambda(g)) \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \wreath S_{n+1}
	\]
	where 
	\[
		\varepsilon_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if $\lambda(s_j^*g): \{i,i+1\} \to \{j,j+1\}$ is order preserving,}\\
						1 & \text{if $\lambda(s_j^*g): \{i,i+1\} \to \{j,j+1\}$ is order reversing.}
				\end{cases}
	\]
	Using the unique factorization property in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$, it is straightforward to verify 
	that the association $g \mapsto \widetilde{\lambda}(g)$ extends to provide a functor
	\[
		\widetilde{\lambda}: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\Delta {\mathfrak W}}
	\]
	commuting with the forgetful functors to ${\mathcal Set}$, which proves (1). The remaining statements
	are easy to verify, the only nonobvious point being that ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}'$ is in fact noncrossed
	simplicial. But this follows from the construction of $\widetilde{\lambda}$: For $g \in
	\mathfrak{G}_n$, the condition $\lambda(g) = \operatorname{id} \in S_{n+1}$ implies that $g^*$ fixes all face maps
	$[n-1] \to [n]$. The condition that all signs $\varepsilon_i$ of the lift
	$\widetilde{\lambda(g)}$ are $0$ implies that $g^*$ fixes all degeneracy maps $[n+1] \to
	[n]$. But this implies that ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}''$ is a simplicial group (cf. Example \ref{exa:deviation}).

nodes.statement: item A parity on a group G is defined to be a homomorphism G to Z/2Z. We obtain a category with parity by passing to groupoids mathcal B G to mathcal BZ/2Z. item Let EuScript D be a category equipped with an involutive functor tau: EuScript D to EuScript D. We may interpret tau as an action of Z/2Z on EuScript D. The corresponding semidirect product Z/2Z ltimes EuScript D to mathcal BZ/2Z is a category with parity.
nodes.raw_latex:
\begin{enumerate}
		\item A {\em parity} on a group $G$ is defined to be a homomorphism $G \to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. We
			obtain a category with parity by passing to groupoids ${\mathcal B} G \to
			{\mathcal B}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
		\item Let ${\EuScript D}$ be a category equipped with an involutive functor $\tau: {\EuScript D} \to {\EuScript D}$.
			We may interpret $\tau$ as an action of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ on ${\EuScript D}$. The corresponding 
			semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \ltimes {\EuScript D} \to {\mathcal B}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is a category with parity.
	\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: We give some examples of categories with parities arising as semidirect products with Z/2Z. item Consider the category EuScript Cat of small categories. The involution tau: EuScript C mapsto EuScript C^op gives rise to a semidirect product Z/2Z ltimes EuScript Cat. We can consider enriched variants of this construction. For example, given a field k, we obtain a semidirect product Z/2Z ltimes EuScript Cat_k where EuScript Cat_k denotes the category of small k-linear categories (categories enriched over Vect_k). item As we have seen above, the simplex category Delta has a natural involution daleth and we obtain a corresponding semidirect product Z/2Z ltimes Delta. item Let EuScript C be any category. nodes.raw_latex:
\label{exas:semi} We give some examples of categories with parities arising as semidirect products with
	$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Consider the category ${\EuScript Cat}$ of small categories. The involution $\tau: {\EuScript C}
			\mapsto {\EuScript C}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ gives rise to a semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \ltimes {\EuScript Cat}$.
			We can consider enriched variants of this construction. For example, given a
			field $\mathbf{k}$, we obtain a semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \ltimes {\EuScript Cat}_\mathbf{k}$ where ${\EuScript Cat}_\mathbf{k}$ denotes the
			category of small $\mathbf{k}$-linear categories (categories enriched over $\operatorname{Vect}_\mathbf{k}$).
		\item As we have seen above, the simplex category $\Delta$ has a natural involution
			$\daleth$ and we obtain a corresponding semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \ltimes \Delta$.
		\item Let ${\EuScript C}$ be any category. The involution $\daleth$ of $\Delta$ induces an
			involution on the category ${\EuScript C}_{\Delta}$ of simplicial objects in ${\EuScript C}$. We
			obtain a semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \ltimes {\EuScript C}_{\Delta}$.
	\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: item From Example (1), we obtain the concept of a twisted group actions on a k-linear category. Explicitly, this means that even group elements act as covariant functors while odd group elements act via contravariant functors. As a special case, given by a k-linear category with one object, we obtain the concept of a twisted group action on an associative k-algebra. item Example (3) provides us with the concept of a twisted group action on a simplicial set (or more generally simplicial object). Here, even group elements act in an the usual orientation preserving way: all face and degeneracy relations are respected. Odd group elements act in an orientation reversing way so that all face and degeneracy relations are reversed according to the involution daleth: Delta to Delta.

		actions on a $\mathbf{k}$-linear category. Explicitly, this means that even group elements act as 
		covariant functors while odd group elements act via contravariant functors. As a special case, given
		by a $\mathbf{k}$-linear category with one object, we obtain the concept of a twisted group action on an
		associative $\mathbf{k}$-algebra. 
	\item Example \ref{exas:semi}(3) provides us with the concept of a twisted group action on a
		simplicial set (or more generally simplicial object). Here, even group elements act
		in an the usual orientation preserving way: all face and degeneracy relations are
		respected. Odd group elements act in an orientation reversing way so that all face
		and degeneracy relations are reversed according to the involution $\daleth: \Delta \to
		\Delta$.
	\end{enumerate}

\label{prop:main} Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a semiconstant crossed simplicial group. Then, for any category ${\EuScript C}$, 
	we have a natural equivalence of categories
	\[
		{\EuScript C}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}} \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \mathfrak{G}_0-{\EuScript C}_{\Delta}, \; K \mapsto K_{| \Delta} 
	\]
	where 
	\[
		\mathfrak{G}_0-{\EuScript C}_{\Delta} = \operatorname{Fun}_{{\mathcal B}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}}({\mathcal B} \mathfrak{G}_0, \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \ltimes {\EuScript C}_{\Delta})
	\]
	denotes the category of simplicial objects in ${\EuScript C}$ equipped with a twisted
	group action of $\mathfrak{G}_0 \to \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(\Delta) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.statement: The cyclic category Lambda has objects langle n rangle, n ge 0, while the set of morphisms from langle m rangle to langle n rangle can be described as follows. Let C_n denote the topological space given by the unit circle in C equipped with the subset of marked points \0, 1, dots, n\, embedded via the map k mapsto exp(2pi i k /(n+1)). A morphism f: langle n rangle to langle m rangle in Lambda is a homotopy class of monotone maps C_m to C_n of degree 1 such that f(\0,1,dots,m\) subset \0,1,dots,n\. The category Delta is contained in Lambda given by restricting to those morphisms f: langle n rangle to langle m rangle such that any homotopy inverse of f, relative to the marked points, maps the oriented arc between m and 0 on C_m into the arc between n and 0 on C_n. The family of groups G associated to Lambda via is the family of cyclic groups \G_n=Z/(n+1)\.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:cyclic}
 	The {\bf cyclic category} $\Lambda$ has objects $\langle n \rangle$, $n \ge 0$, while the set of
	morphisms from $\langle m \rangle$ to $\langle n \rangle$ can be described as follows. Let $C_n$ denote the topological
	space given by the unit circle in $\mathbb{C}$ equipped with the subset of marked points $\{0, 1,
	\dots, n\}$, embedded via the map $k \mapsto \exp(2\pi i k /(n+1))$. A morphism $f: \langle n \rangle \to
	\langle m \rangle$ in $\Lambda$ is a homotopy class of monotone maps $C_m \to C_n$ of degree $1$ such
	that $f(\{0,1,\dots,m\}) \subset \{0,1,\dots,n\}$. The category $\Delta$ is contained in
	$\Lambda$ given by restricting to those morphisms $f: \langle n \rangle \to \langle m \rangle$ such that any homotopy
	inverse of $f$, relative to the marked points, maps the oriented arc between $m$ and $0$ on
	$C_m$ into the arc between $n$ and $0$ on $C_n$.
	The family of groups $\mathfrak{G}$ associated to $\Lambda$ via \eqref{eq:crossed} is the family of cyclic
	groups $\{\mathfrak{G}_n=\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\}$.

\label{ex:dihedral}
 The {\bf dihedral category} $\Xi$ has objects $\overline{\langle n \rangle}$, $n \ge 0$. 
	Morphisms from $\overline{\langle m \rangle}$ to $\overline{\langle n \rangle}$ are homotopy classes of monotone 
	maps $C_m \to C_n$ of degree  $\pm 1$  such that $f(\{0,1,\dots,m\}) \subset
	\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. The category $\Xi$ naturally contains $\Lambda$ and hence also $\Delta$.
	The family of groups $\mathfrak{G}$ associated to $\Xi$ via \eqref{eq:crossed} is the family of dihedral 
	groups
	  \[
	 \mathfrak{G}_n = D_{n+1} = \langle \omega, \tau |\, \omega ^2=1, \tau^{n+1}=1, 
	 \omega\tau\omega^{-1} = \tau^{-1}\rangle 
	 \]	
	 with $|D_{n+1}| = 2(n+1)$.

nodes.statement: The paracyclic category Lambda_infty has objects widetilden, n ge 0. Morphisms from widetildem to widetilden are maps f: Z to Z which preserve the standard linear order and satisfy, for every l in Z, the condition f(l + m+1) = f(l) + n + 1. The category Delta can be found in Lambda_infty by considering only morphisms f:widetildem to widetilden such that \[ f(\0,1,dots, m\) subset \0,1,dots,n\. \] Construction yields the constant family of infinite cyclic groups \G_n=Z\. While this category was introduced in , we borrow the terminology paracyclic from .
nodes.raw_latex:
The {\bf paracyclic category} $\Lambda_{\infty}$ has objects $\widetilde{n}$, $n \ge 0$. 
	Morphisms from $\widetilde{m}$ to $\widetilde{n}$  are maps $f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ which
	preserve the standard linear order and satisfy, for every $l \in \mathbb{Z}$, the condition $f(l +
	m+1) = f(l) + n + 1$. The category $\Delta$ can be found in $\Lambda_{\infty}$ by
	considering only morphisms $f:\widetilde{m} \to \widetilde{n}$ such that 
	\[
	 f(\{0,1,\dots, m\}) \subset 
	\{0,1,\dots,n\}.
	\] 
	Construction \eqref{eq:crossed} yields the constant family
	of infinite cyclic groups $\{\mathfrak{G}_n=\mathbb{Z}\}$. While this category was introduced in
	 \cite{fiedorowicz-loday}, we borrow
	the terminology {\em paracyclic} from \cite{getzler-jones}.

nodes.statement: The paradihedral category Xi_infty has objects widehat n, ngeq 0. Morphisms from widehat m to widehat n are maps f: Z to Z which either preserve or reverse the standard linear order and satisfy, for every l in Z, the condition \[ f(l +m+1) = f(l) + n + 1, if f preserves the order, \\ f(l)-n-1, if f reverses the order. \] Thus Xi_inftysupset Lambda_inftysupsetDelta. Construction yields the constant family of infinite dihedral groups \[ G_n = D_infty = langle omega, tau |\, omega ^2=1, omegatauomega^-1 = tau^-1rangle. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:para-dihedral} 
The {\bf paradihedral category} $\Xi_\infty$ has objects $\widehat n$, $n\geq 0$.
Morphisms from $\widehat m$ to $\widehat n$  are maps $f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ which either preserve or reverse
	 the standard linear order and satisfy, for every $l \in \mathbb{Z}$, the condition 
	 \[
	 f(l +m+1) = \begin{cases} 
	 f(l) + n + 1, \text{ if $f$ preserves the order}, \\
	 f(l)-n-1,\text { if $f$ reverses the order}.
	 \end{cases}
	\]
	Thus $\Xi_\infty\supset \Lambda_\infty\supset\Delta$. 
	Construction \eqref{eq:crossed} yields the constant family
	of infinite dihedral groups 
	  \[
	 \mathfrak{G}_n = D_{\infty} = \langle \omega, \tau |\, \omega ^2=1, \omega\tau\omega^{-1} = \tau^{-1}\rangle. 
	 \]

nodes.statement: The N-subdivided categories Lambda_N, Xi_N. Given a crossed simplicial group DeltaG with the associated simplicial set G, one can form the simplicial set sd_N^*G and ask whether it can be completed to a new crossed simplicial group Deltasd_N^*G. It was observed in that this is indeed so for DeltaG equal to Lambda and Xi. The corresponding crossed simplicial groups will be denoted Lambda_N, Xi_N. They can be defined explicitly as follows. (a) The N-cyclic category Lambda_N has objects widetilden_N, n ge 0. A morphism from widetildem_N to widetilden_N is an equivalence class of maps f: Z to Z which preserve the standard linear order and satisfy, for every l in Z, the condition f(l + m+1) = f(l) + n + 1. A pair of maps f,g are considered equivalent if there exists an integer r such that f - g = rN(n+1). The category Delta can be found in Lambda_N by considering only those morphisms f:widetildem_N to widetilden_N such that \[ f(\0,1,dots, m\) subset \0,1,dots,n\. \] Thus G_n= \Z/N(n+1)Z\. A description of Lambda_N which is more in line with Example can be obtained as follows. Fix an N-fold cover widetildeC to C of the unit circle in C. Then a morphism in Lambda_N between widetildem_N and widetilden_N can be described as a homotopy class of monotone maps C_m to C_n of degree 1, preserving the marked points, together with a lift to widetildeC. (b) The N-dihedral category Xi_N is obtained by modifying the definition of Lambda_N, allowing f to either preserve or reverse the standard linear order and imposing the condition on f(l+m+1) as in Example . We have a topological description analogous to the one for the N-cyclic category.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:subdivided} The {\bf $N$-subdivided categories $\Lambda_N, \Xi_N$.}
 Given a crossed simplicial group $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ with the associated simplicial set $\mathfrak{G}$,
 one can form the simplicial set $\operatorname{sd}_N^*\mathfrak{G}$ and ask whether it can be
 completed to a new crossed simplicial group $\Delta\operatorname{sd}_N^*\mathfrak{G}$. 
 It was observed  in \cite[Ex.7]{fiedorowicz-loday} that this is indeed so
 for $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ equal to $\Lambda$ and $\Xi$.
 The corresponding crossed simplicial groups will be denoted $\Lambda_N, \Xi_N$. 
 They can be defined explicitly as follows.
 
 (a) The {\bf $N$-cyclic category} $\Lambda_{N}$ has objects $\widetilde{n}_N$, $n \ge 0$. A
	morphism from $\widetilde{m}_N$ to $\widetilde{n}_N$ is  an equivalence class of maps 
	$f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ which preserve the standard linear order and satisfy, for every $l \in \mathbb{Z}$, the condition $f(l +
	m+1) = f(l) + n + 1$. A pair of maps $f,g$ are considered equivalent if there exists an integer $r$ such that
	$f - g = rN(n+1)$. The category $\Delta$ can be found in $\Lambda_{N}$ by
	considering only those morphisms $f:\widetilde{m}_N \to \widetilde{n}_N$ such that 
	\[
	f(\{0,1,\dots, m\}) \subset \{0,1,\dots,n\}.
	\]
	Thus $\mathfrak{G}_n= \{\mathbb{Z}/N(n+1)\mathbb{Z}\}$.  
	 
	A description of $\Lambda_N$ which is more in line with Example \ref{ex:cyclic} can be obtained
	as follows. Fix an $N$-fold cover $\widetilde{C} \to C$ of the unit circle in $\mathbb{C}$. Then a
	morphism in $\Lambda_N$ between $\widetilde{m}_N$ and $\widetilde{n}_N$ can be described as a homotopy class of
	monotone maps $C_m$ to $C_n$ of degree $1$, preserving the marked points, together with a lift to $\widetilde{C}$.
	
	(b) The {\bf $N$-dihedral category} $\Xi_N$ is obtained by modifying the definition of $\Lambda_N$, 
	 allowing $f$ to either preserve or
	reverse the standard linear order and imposing the condition on $f(l+m+1)$ as in Example 
	\ref{ex:para-dihedral}. We have a topological description analogous to the one for the
	$N$-cyclic category.

To describe morphisms, we first introduce the quaternionic groups \[ Q_n \,\,=\,\, langle w, tau |\, w^2=tau^n , tau^2n=w^4=1, wtau w^-1 = tau^-1rangle, |Q_n|=4n. \] Here ngeq 1 is an integer. Thus Q_1=Z/4. Let H be the skew field of quaternions. For any r, we denote by mu_r subset C^* subset H^* the group of rth roots of 1. Then Q_n, ngeq 2, can be identified with the subgroup in H^* generated by mu_2n and j. In other words, Q_n is, for ngeq 2, a finite subgroup in SU_2 of type D in the standard ADE classification (and in that context is also sometimes referred to, confusingly, as the ``dihedral group"). Another traditional name for Q_n is the ``dicyclic group" . We have the central extension 1to Z/2longrightarrow Q_nbuildrel pi_n over longrightarrow D_nto 1, pi_n(omega) = omega For ngeq 3, D_n embeds into the group of automorphisms of mu_nsimeq Z/n, while Q_nsubsetH^* normalizes mu_n, so pi_n is obtained by looking at the conjugation action of Q_n. The morphisms of nabla are defined to be generated by the morphisms in Delta and by elements of the groups Autnolimits_nabla(check n):=Q_n+1 subject to the relations spelled out in , Prop. 6.3.4(e) (proof). Thus, for nabla we have \[ G_n = Q_n+1, |G_n|= 4(n+1). \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:quaternionic}
The {\bf quaternionic category} $\nabla$ has objects $\check n$, $n\geq 0$.
To describe morphisms, we first introduce the {\em quaternionic groups}
\[
   Q_n  \,\,=\,\,  \langle w, \tau |\, w^2=\tau^n , \tau^{2n}=w^4=1, w\tau w^{-1} = \tau^{-1}\rangle,
   \quad |Q_n|=4n.
\]
    Here $n\geq 1$ is an integer.  Thus $Q_1=\mathbb{Z}/4$. Let $\mathbb{H}$  be the skew field of quaternions.
    For any $r$, we denote by   $\mu_r \subset \mathbb{C}^* \subset \mathbb{H}^*$ the group of $r$th roots of 1.
    Then $Q_n$, $n\geq 2$, can be identified with the subgroup in $\mathbb{H}^*$ generated by $\mu_{2n}$
    and $j$. In other words,   $Q_n$ is, for $n\geq 2$, a finite subgroup in $SU_2$ of type $D$ in
    the standard ADE classification (and in that context is also sometimes referred to, confusingly,
    as the ``dihedral group").  Another  traditional name for $Q_n$ is the {``dicyclic group"}
    \cite[\S 7.2]{coxeter}.  We have the central extension 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:p_n} 1\to
	    \mathbb{Z}/2\longrightarrow Q_n\buildrel \pi_n \over \longrightarrow D_n\to 1, \quad \pi_n(\omega) = \omega
    \end{equation} 
    For $n\geq 3$, $D_n$ embeds into the group of automorphisms of $\mu_n\simeq
    \mathbb{Z}/n$, while $Q_n\subset\mathbb{H}^*$ normalizes $\mu_n$, so $\pi_n$ is obtained by looking at the
    conjugation action of $Q_n$.

 The morphisms of $\nabla$ are defined to be generated by the morphisms in $\Delta$
 and by elements of the groups $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_\nabla(\check n):=Q_{n+1}$ subject to the relations
 spelled out in \cite{loday}, Prop. 6.3.4(e) (proof). Thus, for $\nabla$ we have
 \[
 \mathfrak{G}_n = Q_{n+1}, \quad |\mathfrak{G}_n|= 4(n+1). 
 \]

\label{prop:summary-covers}
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Suppose we are given subgroups $\widetilde P\subset P$, $\widetilde A\subset A$ so that $\widetilde A$ 
is $P$-invariant. For the existence of a connective covering $\widetilde G$ realizing $\widetilde P$ and $\widetilde A$

be $0$.

simply connected), if and only if $\gamma_G=0$.

spaces, then pullback under $f$ gives an equivalence of categories
\[
f^*: \operatorname{Con}(G_2)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Con}(G_1). 
\]
\end{itemize}

We note that algebraic data $(P,A,\gamma)$ as above appear in the classification of the following related
types of objects:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item {\bf Connected homotopy $2$-types,} i.e., homotopy types of connected CW-complexes $X$
with $\pi_{> 2}(X,x)=0$. In this context, $P=\pi_1(X,x)$, $A=\pi_2(X,x)$. 
A topological group $G$ produces such $X$ by forming the classifying space $BG$ and then 
killing $\pi_{> 2}$.

It corresponds to the paradihedral category Xi_infty. item Consider the group \[ P \,\,=\,\,bigl\ qinH^* bigl| \,\, |q|=1, q S^1 q^-1 subset S^1 bigr\. \] Here S^1 is considered as the unit circle subgroup in C^*subsetH^*. In other words, P is the normalizer of a maximal torus in SU(2). Like O(2), the group P has pi_0=Z/2 and P_e= S^1, but the corresponding extension of Z/2 by S^1 is different from the one provided by O(2). Similarly to , looking at the conjugation action gives a central extension \[ 1to Z/2longrightarrow P buildrel pi over longrightarrow O(2)to 1 \] with pi a proper covering. This makes P into a planar Lie group. It corresponds to the quaternionic category nabla. item Let Ngeq 1. We denote the unique N-fold proper covering of SO(2) by \[ 1to Z/N longrightarrow Spin_N(2)buildrel phi_Nover longrightarrow SO(2) to 1. \] As an abstract Lie group, Spin_N(2) is identified with SO(2), and phi_N is the Nth power homomorphism. The group Spin_N(2) corresponds to the N-cyclic category Lambda_N. item Let us represent elements of O(2) = (Z/2)ltimes S^1 as pairs (alpha, z)=alphacdot z with alphainZ/2, zin S^1, so that alpha zalpha^-1 = z^-1. Then the map \[ f_N: O(2)longrightarrow O(2), (alpha, z)mapsto (alpha, z^N). \] is a (continuous) homomorphism and, moreover, a proper covering with kernel Z/N. We denote this covering \[ 1to Z/N longrightarrow Pin^+_N(2) buildrel p_N^+ overlongrightarrow O(2)to 1 \] Thus Pin^+_N(2)=O(2) as an abstract Lie group, and p_N^+=f_N. The planar Lie group Pin^+_N(2) corresponds to the N-dihedral category Xi_N. item If N=2M is even, then the composition Pbuildrel pi overto O(2) buildrel f_Moverto O(2) is a proper covering with kernel Z/N. We denote this covering \[ 1to Z/N longrightarrow Pin^-_N(2) buildrel p_N^- overlongrightarrow O(2)to 1 \] Thus Pin^-_N(2)=Q_infty as an abstract Lie group, and p_N^-=f_Mpi. The planar Lie group Pin^-_N(2) corresponds to the M-quaternionic category nabla_M.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:planar}
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
	    \item The group $SO(2)$ corresponds to the cyclic category $\Lambda$. 
	    \item The group $O(2)$ corresponds to the dihedral category $\Xi$. 
	    \item We denote by $\widetilde{SO}(2)\to SO(2)$ the universal covering of $SO(2)\simeq S^1$.
		It corresponds to the paracyclic category $\Lambda_\infty$.
	    \item We denote 
		   \[
		   \widetilde O(2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow O(2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes S^1
		   \]
		   the proper covering  of the semi-direct product induced from the universal covering $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$.
		   It corresponds to the paradihedral category $\Xi_\infty$. 
	   \item Consider the group
		     \[
		  P \,\,=\,\,\bigl\{ q\in\mathbb{H}^* \bigl| \,\, |q|=1, q S^1 q^{-1} \subset S^1 \bigr\}.
		  \]
		  Here $S^1$ is considered as the unit circle subgroup in $\mathbb{C}^*\subset\mathbb{H}^*$.
		   In other words, $P$ is the normalizer of a maximal torus in $SU(2)$. 
		   Like $O(2)$, the group $P$ has  $\pi_0=\mathbb{Z}/2$ and  $P_e= S^1$, but the
		   corresponding
		  extension of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ by $S^1$  is different from the one provided by $O(2)$. 
		  Similarly to \eqref{eq:p_n},  looking at the conjugation action gives a central extension
		   \[
		   1\to \mathbb{Z}/2\longrightarrow P \buildrel \pi \over \longrightarrow O(2)\to 1
		   \]
		   with $\pi$ a proper covering. This makes  $P$ into a planar Lie group.
		   It corresponds to the quaternionic category $\nabla$. 

	   \item Let $N\geq 1$. We denote the unique $N$-fold proper covering of $SO(2)$ by 
		   \[
		   1\to \mathbb{Z}/N \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spin}_N(2)\buildrel \phi_N\over \longrightarrow SO(2) \to 1.
		   \]
		  As an abstract Lie group, $\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$ is identified with $SO(2)$, and $\phi_N$
		  is the $N$th power homomorphism. The group $\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$ corresponds to the
		  $N$-cyclic category $\Lambda_N$.

	    \item Let us represent elements of $O(2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes S^1$
		   as pairs $(\alpha, z)=\alpha\cdot z$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}/2$, $z\in S^1$, so that 
		  $\alpha z\alpha^{-1} = z^{-1}$.   Then the map
		     \[
		  f_N: O(2)\longrightarrow O(2), \quad (\alpha, z)\mapsto (\alpha, z^N).
		   \]
		   is a (continuous) homomorphism and, moreover, a proper covering with kernel $\mathbb{Z}/N$. 
		   We denote this covering
		   \[
		   1\to \mathbb{Z}/N \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pin}^+_N(2) \buildrel p_N^+ \over\longrightarrow O(2)\to 1
		   \]
		   Thus $ \operatorname{Pin}^+_N(2)=O(2)$ as an abstract Lie group, and $p_N^+=f_N$. 
		   The planar Lie group $\operatorname{Pin}^+_N(2)$ corresponds to the $N$-dihedral category $\Xi_N$.
	   \item If $N=2M$ is even, then 
		    the composition $P\buildrel \pi \over\to O(2) \buildrel f_M\over\to O(2)$
		 is a proper covering with kernel $\mathbb{Z}/N$. We denote this covering
		  \[
		   1\to \mathbb{Z}/N \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pin}^-_N(2) \buildrel p_N^- \over\longrightarrow O(2)\to 1
		   \]
		   Thus $ \operatorname{Pin}^-_N(2)=Q_\infty$ as an abstract Lie group, and $p_N^-=f_M\pi$. 
		    The planar Lie group $\operatorname{Pin}^-_{N}(2)$ corresponds to the $M$-quaternionic category
		    $\nabla_M$. 
\end{enumerate}

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:crossed-groups}
     \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] Let $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ be any crossed simplicial group. Then the geometric realization $|\mathfrak{G}|$
    of the simplicial set $\mathfrak{G}$ has a natural group structure, making it a topological group.
    Further, the geometric realization $|\operatorname{N} (\Delta\mathfrak{G})|$ of the nerve of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$
    is homotopy equivalent to the classifying space $B |\mathfrak{G}|$. 
    
    \item[(b)]  Let $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ be a  planar crossed simplicial group. Then:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(b1)]  $|\mathfrak{G}|=G$ is the
    planar Lie group corresponding to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ in Table \ref{table:corr}. In particular, there
    is a covering $p: G\to O(2)$. 
    
    \item[(b2)] The group $\mathfrak{G}_n$ is identified with the subgroup $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})$,
    where $D_{n+1}$ is embedded into $O(2)=(\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes S^1$ as
    $(\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes\mu_{n+1}$. 
   \end{enumerate}
    
    \item[(c)] Let $X:\Delta\mathfrak{G}^{\operatorname{op}}\to{\mathcal Set}$ be any $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-set. Then $|i^*X|$, the geometric
    realization of $X$ considered as a simplicial set, has a natural $G$-action. 
    
    \item[(d)] The homotopy category of $G$-spaces can be identified with the localization 
    of  the category $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta\mathfrak{G}^{\operatorname{op}}, {\mathcal Set})$ along morphisms which give homotopy equivalences
    of the induced simplicial sets. 
     
    \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: (a) was shown by Fiedorowicz and Loday . The identification of |G| in the examples of (b) is also immediate from their considerations. The remaining parts are well known in the cyclic and paracyclic cases Delta G=Lambda, Lambda_infty, and were extended by Dunn to the dihedral and quaternionic cases. The N-subdivided cases can be deduced from these using the fact that sd_N^* does not change the geometric realization. The paradihedral case can be deduced from the paracyclic one by identifying Xi_infty with the semi-direct product of Z/2 and Lambda_infty. We leave the remaining details to the reader.

\label{prop:orient-G-0}
Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a planar crossed simplicial group with the corresponding planar Lie group $p: G \to O(2)$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Let $O(1)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ be embedded into $O(2)$ in the standard way. Then $\mathfrak{G}_0$ is identified,
as a group with parity, with the preimage of $O(1)$ in $G$, so we have the Cartesian square
\[
\xymatrix{
\mathfrak{G}_0\ar[r]^\epsilon \ar[d]^{\hskip -.7cm \rho} & G\ar[d]^p\\
\mathbb{Z}/2=O(1) \ar[r]& O(2). 
}
\]
\item[(b)] Explicitly, the canonical parities of $\mathfrak{G}_0 = \mathbb{Z}, (\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes \mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}/N, D_N, Q_N$
are given as follows:  
 the groups  $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/N$  are equipped with the trivial homomorphism to
 $\mathbb{Z}/2$, and the group  $D_N$ and $Q_N$ with homomorphisms
\[
 \begin{gathered}
   \rho_D: D_N\longrightarrow  \mathbb{Z}/2, \quad \rho_D(\omega)=\overline 1, \,\,\rho_D(\tau)=\overline 0, 
 \\
 \rho_Q: Q_N\longrightarrow  \mathbb{Z}/2, \quad \rho_Q(w)=\overline 1, \,\,\rho_Q(\tau)=\overline 0,
 \end{gathered}
 \]
 and $(\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}$ with the projection to $\mathbb{Z}/2$. 
\end{enumerate}

\label{thm:G-nerve}
Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be any crossed simplicial group. Equip $\mathfrak{G}_0$ with its canonical parity.
Then to each small category ${\EuScript C}$ with a twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action, there is an associated
${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set $\operatorname{N}^{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}({\EuScript C})$ called the {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-nerve} of ${\EuScript C}$ such that
\[
	\operatorname{N}^{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}({\EuScript C})_n = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak{G}_0-{\EuScript Cat}}(\operatorname{FC}({\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^n_{|\Delta}), {\EuScript C}).
\]

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:hochschild}
Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a planar crossed simplicial group. Let $A$ be a unital associative algebra with a 
twisted action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$. Then the collection of vector spaces
  \[
 C_\bullet(A) =   \bigl\{ C_n(A) = A^{\otimes (n+1)}\bigr\}_{n\geq 0},
  \]
given by the terms of the Hochschild complex of $A$, naturally forms a $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-vector space. 
In particular, the group $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts on $C_n(A)$.

nodes.statement: The cosimplicial structure is obtained by letting face maps act by insertion of 1 and degeneracy maps act by multiplication in A. Let us construct an action of G_n on A^otimes (n+1). Consider the wreath product \[ S_n+1wr G_0 := S_n+1ltimes G_0^n+1, \] where the action of S_n+1 on G_0^n+1 is by permuting the Cartesian factors. Note that we have a projection map S_n+1wrG_0 to S_n+1. We now claim that the homomorphism lambda_n: G_nto S_n+1 from Proposition has a natural lifting to a homomorphism \[ L_n: G_n longrightarrow S_n+1wr G_0. \] Indeed, by the canonical factorization \[ Hom_Delta G([0], [n]) = G_0 timesHom_Delta([0], [n]), \] and G_n acts on this set on the left by composition of morphisms in Delta G. We see, first, that the action of any ginG_n takes any fiber of the projection to Hom_Delta([0], [n]) to another fiber. The induced permutation of these fibers is precisely lambda_n(g)in S_n+1. Second, if we identify each fiber with G_0, then the identification of one fiber with another is given by the left multiplication with some element of G_0, These elements, together with lambda_n(g), give the desired L_n(g)in S_n+1wr G_0. Since G_0 acts on A as a vector space, we have the natural action of S_n+1wrG_0 on A^otimes(n+1) which combines the permutations of the tensor factors and action of G_0 on each factor. We pull this action back along L_n to get a G_n-action on A^otimes(n+1). The compatibility of these actions with the simplicial structure is verified straightforwardly.
nodes.raw_latex:
The cosimplicial structure is obtained by letting face maps act by insertion of $1$ and degeneracy
maps act by multiplication in $A$. Let us construct an action of $\mathfrak{G}_n$  on $A^{\otimes (n+1)}$.
Consider the wreath product
\[
S_{n+1}\wr \mathfrak{G}_0 := S_{n+1}\ltimes \mathfrak{G}_0^{n+1},
\]
where the action of $S_{n+1}$ on $\mathfrak{G}_0^{n+1}$ is by permuting the Cartesian factors. 
Note that we have a projection map $S_{n+1}\wr\mathfrak{G}_0 \to S_{n+1}$. We now claim that the
homomorphism $\lambda_n: \mathfrak{G}_n\to S_{n+1}$ from Proposition \ref{prop:forget} has a natural lifting
to a homomorphism
\[
L_n: \mathfrak{G}_n \longrightarrow S_{n+1}\wr \mathfrak{G}_0. 
\]
Indeed, by the canonical factorization
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n]) = \mathfrak{G}_0 \times\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n]),
\]
and $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts on this set on the left by composition of morphisms in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.  We see, first,
that the action of any $g\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ takes any fiber of the projection to $\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n])$ to
another fiber. The induced permutation of these fibers is precisely $\lambda_n(g)\in S_{n+1}$.
Second, if we identify each fiber with $\mathfrak{G}_0$, then the identification of one fiber with another
is given by the left multiplication with some element of $\mathfrak{G}_0$, These elements, together with
$\lambda_n(g)$, give the desired $L_n(g)\in S_{n+1}\wr \mathfrak{G}_0$. 

Since $\mathfrak{G}_0$ acts on $A$ as a vector space, we have the natural action of $S_{n+1}\wr\mathfrak{G}_0$ on
$A^{\otimes(n+1)}$ which combines the permutations of the tensor factors and action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ on
each factor. We pull this action back along $L_n$ to get a $\mathfrak{G}_n$-action on $A^{\otimes(n+1)}$.
The compatibility of these actions with the simplicial structure is verified straightforwardly.

nodes.raw_latex:
The Hochschild complex of an associative algebra is usually constructed as the
	totalization of a {\em simplicial} $\mathbf{k}$-vector space. This simplicial object can be obtained
	by precomposing the functor ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \to \operatorname{Vect}$ from Theorem \ref{thm:hochschild} with
	\[
		\Delta^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \overset{D}{\longrightarrow} {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} 
	\]
	where $D$ denotes a self-duality of the category ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ (cf. Corollary \ref{cor:duality}
	below).

nodes.statement: Elements of H^0_Delta G(A) = Hom_Delta G-Vect( C_bullet(A), k) will be called Delta G-traces on A. Thus a Delta G-trace beta is a collection of multilinear forms beta_n: A^otimes(n+1), k), ngeq 0. The condition that beta is a morphism of cosimplicial vector spaces, means that all the beta_n are expressible through the linear form beta_1: \[ beta_n(a_0, a_1, cdots, a_n) = beta_1(a_0a_1cdots a_n). \] The further conditions on beta_1 express G_n-invariance of beta_n for ngeq 0. Note that these conditions do not necessarily imply that the bilinear form beta_2 is symmetric.
nodes.raw_latex:
Elements of $H^0_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(A) = \operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Vect}}( C_\bullet(A), \mathbf{k})$ will be called {\em
${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-traces} on $A$. Thus a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-trace $\beta$ is a collection of multilinear forms $\beta_n:
A^{\otimes(n+1)}, \mathbf{k})$, $n\geq 0$. The condition that $\beta$ is a morphism of cosimplicial vector
spaces, means that all the $\beta_n$ are expressible through the linear form $\beta_1$:
\[
\beta_n(a_0, a_1, \cdots, a_n) = \beta_1(a_0a_1\cdots a_n). 
\]
The further conditions on $\beta_1$ express $\mathfrak{G}_n$-invariance of $\beta_n$ for $n\geq 0$.
Note that these conditions do not necessarily imply that the bilinear form $\beta_2$ is symmetric.

nodes.statement: (a) Let Delta G be any planar simplicial group with corresponding planar Lie group G. We expect that the theory of Delta G-structured graphs developed in S can be used to generalize the results of as follows: A Delta G-Frobenius algebra gives rise to a numerical invariant defined on G-structured surfaces without boundary and to a TQFT on G-structured 2-dimensional cobordisms (with marked points as in S allowed in both cases and with additional constraints of commutativity removing the dependence on marking points). vskip .1cm (b) Further, one can extend the concept of a Delta G-Frobenius algebra to the case of associative dg (or A_infty) algebras, and dg (or A_infty) categories also allowing the forms beta_1 and beta_2 to have some degree dneq 0 as in . The corresponding ``d-dimensional Delta G-Calabi-Yau algebras and categories" should then give cohomology classes on moduli spaces of marked G-structured surfaces generalizing . We leave both these directions to future work.

	\ref{sec:structuredgraphs} can be used to generalize the results of \cite{kock,
	alex-natanzon, novak-runkel} as follows: A ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-Frobenius algebra gives rise to a numerical
	invariant defined on $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces without boundary and to a TQFT on

	\ref{subsec:c-infty} allowed in both cases and with additional constraints of commutativity
	removing the dependence on marking points).

	associative dg (or $A_{\infty}$) algebras, and dg (or $A_\infty$) categories also allowing

	\cite{kontsevich-feynman}. The corresponding ``$d$-dimensional ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-Calabi-Yau algebras and
	categories" should then give cohomology classes on moduli spaces of marked $\mathbb{G}$-structured
	surfaces generalizing \cite{costello-TFT, kontsevich-feynman}.

	We leave both these directions to future work.

nodes.raw_latex:
Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a crossed simplicial group. A {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set} is a pair $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$, where:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $I$ is  a nonempty finite set of some cardinality $n+1$, $n\geq 0$. 
\item[(2)] $\mathcal{O}(I)$ is a right $\mathfrak{G}_n$-torsor together with a map
\[
\rho: \mathcal{O}(I) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}\bigl( \{0,1,\dots, n\}, I \bigr)
\]
which is equivariant with respect to the homomorphism $\lambda_n: \mathfrak{G}_n\to S_{n+1}$
from Proposition \ref {prop:forget}.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: A morphism of Delta G-structured sets \[ psi: (I', O(I'))longrightarrow (I, O(I)), |I'|=n'+1, \, |I|=n+1, \] is a datum of morphisms \[ left\ psi_f,f'inHom_Delta G([n'], [n]) \; big| \; f'in O(I'), finO(I)right\, \] satisfying, for every g in G_n, g' in G_n', the equivariance condition \[ psi_fg, f'g' = g^-1 circ psi_f, f'circ g'. \] The composition of two morphisms \[ (I'', O(I'')) oversetpsi'longrightarrow (I', O(I')) oversetpsilongrightarrow (I, O(I)) \] is defined by the formula \[ (psipsi')_f, f'' = psi_f,f' circ psi'_f', f'' \] where the right hand is independent on f'.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defi:dgstructure}
A morphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets 
\[
\psi: (I', \mathcal{O}(I'))\longrightarrow (I, \mathcal{O}(I)), \quad |I'|=n'+1, \, |I|=n+1, 
\]
is a datum of morphisms
\[
	\left\{ \psi_{f,f'}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([n'], [n]) \; \big| \; \text{$f'\in \mathcal{O}(I')$,
	$f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$}\right\},
\]
satisfying, for every $g \in \mathfrak{G}_{n}$, $g' \in \mathfrak{G}_{n'}$, the equivariance condition
\[
	\psi_{fg, f'g'} = g^{-1} \circ \psi_{f, f'}\circ g'.
\]
The composition of two morphisms
\[
	(I'', \mathcal{O}(I'')) \overset{\psi'}{\longrightarrow}  (I', \mathcal{O}(I')) \overset{\psi}{\longrightarrow} (I, \mathcal{O}(I))
\]
is defined by the formula
\[
(\psi\psi')_{f, f''} = \psi_{f,f'} \circ \psi'_{f', f''}
\]
where the right hand is independent on $f'$.

nodes.statement: Consider the crossed simplicial group Delta G = Xi given by the dihedral category. We have G_0 = G_0^0 = Z/2Z so that, for a singleton set I, the category G/I has a single isomorphism class of objects and each object has automorphism group Z/2Z. We have G_1 = Z/2Z times Z/2Z and G_1^0 = Z/2Z so that, on a given set I of cardinality 2, we have one isomorphism class of objects in G/I, each object having automorphism group Z/2Z. For |I| = n+1 with n ge 2, the objects of G/I have trivial automorphism group, and there are fracn!2 isomorphism classes.

	have $\mathfrak{G}_0 = \mathfrak{G}_0^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ so that, for a singleton set $I$, the category $\mathcal{G}/I$ has a
	single isomorphism class of objects and each object has automorphism group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.  We have
	$\mathfrak{G}_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathfrak{G}_1^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ so that, on a given set $I$ of cardinality

	group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. For $|I| = n+1$ with $n \ge 2$, the objects of $\mathcal{G}/I$ have trivial
	automorphism group, and there are $\frac{n!}{2}$ isomorphism classes.

To define the map psi^*: O(I)toO(I') associated to psi, we fix finO(I), choose and arbitrary f'inO(I') and interpret them as vertical isomorphisms in the diagram \[ xymatrix (I', O(I')) ar[rr]^psi && (I, O(I)) \\ epsilon[n'] ar[u]^f' ar[rr]^psi_f, f' = f^-1circpsicirc f' && epsilon[n] ar[u]_f \\epsilon[n']ar[u]^g' ar[urr]_phi \] Next, we define phi and g' in the diagram via the canonical factorization psi_f, f' = phicirc g' with phiinDelta, g'inG_n', and set psi^*(f)=f'circ g'. The result is independent of f' in virtue of the equivariance condition on the datum psi=(psi_f, f'). This defines the pair (psi_*, psi^*) associated to psi. of the functor $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$. To define the map $\psi^*: \mathcal{O}(I)\to\mathcal{O}(I')$ associated to $\psi$,
we fix $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$, choose and arbitrary $f'\in\mathcal{O}(I')$ and interpret them as vertical
isomorphisms in the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
(I', \mathcal{O}(I')) \ar[rr]^\psi && (I, \mathcal{O}(I))
\\
\epsilon[n']
\ar[u]^{f'} 
 \ar[rr]^{\psi_{f, f'} = f^{-1}\circ\psi\circ f' }&& \epsilon[n]
 \ar[u]_f
 \\\epsilon[n']\ar[u]^{g'} 
 \ar[urr]_\phi

Next, we define $\phi$ and $g'$ in the diagram via the canonical factorization
$\psi_{f, f'} = \phi\circ g'$ with $\phi\in\Delta$, $g'\in\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$, and set $\psi^*(f)=f'\circ g'$. The result is independent
of $f'$ in virtue of the equivariance condition on the datum $\psi=(\psi_{f, f'})$.

	that $\leq$ can be identified with the unique monotone bijection $\sigma:
	\{0,1,\dots, n\}\to I$, where $|I|= n+1$. We then define the $\mathfrak{G}_n$-torsor $\mathcal{O}_{\sigma}$ to
	be $\mathfrak{G}_n$, and the map $\rho$ to be the composition

	 \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}\bigl(
	\{0,1,\dots, n\},  I\bigr). 
	\]
	Denoting by ${\bf\Delta}$ the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, we can
	view the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure as a functor ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta} \to\mathcal{G}$ extending
	$i:\Delta \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.

\label{prop:model-G/I}
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)]
For linear orders on $I$ given by bijections $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$, we have
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{G}/I}((I, \mathcal{O}_{\sigma_1}), (I, \mathcal{O}_{\sigma_2})) \cong \bigl\{ g\in\mathfrak{G}_n \bigl| \,\, \lambda_n(g)
= \sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2\bigr\},
\]
and the composition of morphisms corresponds to the multiplication in $\mathfrak{G}_n$. 

\item[(b)] Every object $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ of $\mathcal{G}/I$ is isomorphic  to an object of the form $(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)$,
so the category with objects  $(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)$ and morphisms defined by the right hand side of the identification
in (a), is equivalent to $\mathcal{G}/I$. 
\end{itemize}

Let $u: I'\hookrightarrow I$ be an embedding of nonempty finite sets. Then there is a functor
\[
\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}: \mathcal{G}/I \longrightarrow\mathcal{G}/I'
\]
called {\em restriction of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structures from $I$ to $I'$}, with the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] For each ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure $\mathcal{O}(I)$ on $I$ the map $u$    extends to a canonical
morphism in $\mathcal{G}$
\[
\psi^u: \operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(I, \mathcal{O}(I))\longrightarrow (I, \mathcal{O}(I)).
\]
\item[(b)] For a triple of composable embeddings $I''\hookrightarrow I'\hookrightarrow I$ we have a canonical
isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I''} \,\,\cong \,\, \operatorname{Res}\nolimits^{I'}_{I''}\circ \operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}. 
\]
\end{itemize}

We use the model of $\mathcal{G}/I$ from Proposition \ref{prop:model-G/I}. Given a total order $\leq $ on $I$,
it restricts to a total order on $I'$, and so we have a diagram
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comm-diagr-emb}
\xymatrix{
\{0,1,\dots, n'\} 
\ar[d]_{\sigma'}
\ar[r]^\phi& \{0,1, \dots, n\}\ar[d]^\sigma
\\
I'\ar[r]_u& I,
}
\end{equation}
in which $\psi, u$ are monotone embeddings, and $\sigma,\sigma'$ are monotone bijections. We define on objects
$\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)=(I', \mathcal{O}_{\sigma'})$. 

Further, let $g\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ be such that $\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2$, where 
$\sigma_1, \sigma_2: \{0,1, \dots, n\}\to I$ are the bijections corresponding to two total orders
$\leq^1, \leq^2$ on $I$. Let $\sigma'_1, \sigma'_2: \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\to I'$ be the
bijections corresponding to the restrictions of $\leq^1, \leq^2$ to $I'$. We the have two commutative
diagrams as in \eqref{eq:comm-diagr-emb}, whose arrows we denote $u, \sigma'_\nu, \sigma_\nu, \phi_\nu$,
$\nu=1,2$. 

We claim, first of all, that $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$. Indeed, consider the canonical diagram in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$
\[
\xymatrix{
[n']\ar[d]_{\phi_1^*g}
\ar[r]^{g^*\phi_1}&[n]
\ar[d]^g
\\
[n']\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& [n]
}
\]
defining $g^*\phi_1$ and apply the functor $\lambda$ to it. Because of the assumptions on $g$, the resulting diagram
in ${\bf FSet}$ is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:2.1.11}
\xymatrix{
\{0,1,\dots, n'\}
\ar[d]_{\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)}
\ar[r]^{\phi_2}& \{0,1,\dots, n\}
\ar[d]^{\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma^2}
\\
\{0,1,\dots, n'\}\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& \{0,1,\dots, n\},
}
\end{equation}
whence $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.

We further claim that

	of categories. In particular, the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ is equivalent to ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.

\label{lem:pi0} Let $n \ge 0$ and consider the standard circle $S^1$ equipped with the standard subset
	$[n] \subset S^1$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Consider the subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \subset { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1)$ of homeomorphisms
			preserving which preserve the standard subset $[n]$ of $(n+1)$st roots of
			unity. Let $H_n$ be the pullback 
			\[ 
				\xymatrix{ H_n\ar[d] \ar[r]&{ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1) \ar[d]^{p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}} \\ 
				{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \ar[r]&{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1).  } 
			\] 
			Then each connected component of $H_n$ is contractible
			and there is a canonical group isomorphism $\pi_0(H_n) \cong \mathfrak{G}_0$. 
		\item Let $(C,J)$ be a $G$-structured marked circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure
			group along $ p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. Consider the subset ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J)) \subset { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ 
			consisting of homeomorphisms which map $[n]$ into $J$ and let 
			$\rho_J: F_J \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J))$ denote the restriction of
			$\rho$. Then the set $\pi_0(F_J)$ is a $\pi_0(H_n)$-torsor, equipped with a
			natural equivariant map 
			\[
				\rho_{\pi_0(J)}: \pi_0(F_J) \to \pi_0(J)
			\]
			making $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set.
	\end{enumerate}

The argument is similar to that of \cite{drinfeld:cyclic}. 
 That is, let $\bf\Delta$ be the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, and ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta}\to \mathcal{G}$
 be the functor of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure, extending $i$ (Example \ref{ex:DG-closure}). A simplicial set $Y$ can
 be seen as a contravariant functor $Y: {\bf\Delta}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and, as pointed out in Formula (1.1) of
 \cite {drinfeld:cyclic},
 \[
 |Y|\,\,=\,\,\varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, Y\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr), 
 \]
 where $F$ runs over finite subsets of $[0,1]$, and $\pi_0([0,1]-F)$ is equipped by the total order
 induced by that on $[0,1]$. 
 
 Now, if $X$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set, we can view $X$ as a contravariant functor $\mathcal{G}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and identify
 \[
 \begin{gathered}
 |i^*X| \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, ({\bf i}^*X)\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr) \,\,=\,\,
 \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0([0,1]-F))\bigr) \,\,= \\
=\,\,   \varinjlim\limits_{1\in F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr) \,\,=\,\,
  \,\,  \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr).
  \end{gathered}
 \]
 Here we view $S^1$ as obtained from $[0,1]$ by identifying $0$ and $1$ into one point $1\in S^1$ and as equipped
 with the standard ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure. Each set $\pi_0(S^1-F)$ is then equipped with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure
 by Corollary \ref{cor:structured-circle-orders}. Now, the last colimit is manifestly acted upon by
 ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$. \qed

nodes.name: (total) cyclic order
nodes.statement: A (total) cyclic order on a finite set J of cardinality n is the choice of a simply transitive action of the group Z/nZ. Note that a cyclic order on the set J is uniquely determined by specifying for every element j its successor j + 1.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:totalcyclic} A {\em (total) cyclic order} on a finite set $J$ of cardinality $n$ is 
the choice of a simply transitive action of the group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Note that a cyclic order on the set $J$ 
is uniquely determined by specifying for every element $j$ its {\em successor} $j + 1$.

nodes.statement: item Any set of cardinality le 2 has a unique cyclic order. A cyclic order on a set J of cardinality 3 is the same as an orientation of the triangle |Delta^J|. item Every subset of a cyclically ordered set J has a canonical cyclic order. item Any finite linearly ordered set J carries a canonical cyclic order where the successor of each nonmaximal element of J is its successor with respect to the linear order and the minimal element is the successor of the maximal element. We say that this cyclic order is the cyclic closure of the linear order on J. item More generally, given a cyclically ordered finite set K and a map of finite sets f: J to K where each fiber of f is equipped with a linear order, we can define the lexicographic cyclic order on J as follows. First note, that the set of fibers of f is canonically identified with K and hence carries a cyclic order. Therefore, every fiber has a successor fiber. Now the cyclic order on J is given as follows: For every element j which is nonmaximal in its fiber, we define the successor j +1 to be the successor with respect to the specified linear order of the fiber. If j is maximal in its fiber, we define its successor to be the minimal element of the successor fiber. Here the convention is to skip all empty fibers. The previous example is then given by the case when K is a point, equipped with its unique cyclic order.

			previous example is then given by the case when $K$ is a point, equipped

	\end{enumerate}

That is, two such embeddings u: Jto C and u':Jto C' are identified iff there is an orientation preserving homeomorphism phi: Cto C' such that phi u=u'. nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:cyclic-orders}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $C$ be a circle.
Then $C^3_\neq = C^3-\bigcup_{i\neq j} \{x_i=x_j\}$ has two connected components which are
in bijection with  orientations of $C$. The ``anti-clockwise" component corrresponding to a
choice of orientation contains triples $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$  with $x_i$ following very closely
each other in the orientation direction. The closure $\lambda$ of this component is a total
cyclic order on $C$.  In particular, the standard oriented circle $S^1 =
\{|z|=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}$ has a canonical cyclic order. 
 
This implies that a total cyclic order on a finite set $J$ can be defined as an  homeomorphism class
of embeddings of $J$ into oriented circles. That is, two such embeddings $u: J\to C$  and $u':J\to
C'$  are identified  iff there is an orientation preserving homeomorphism $\phi: C\to C'$ such that
$\phi u=u'$. It is now easy to verify that a total cyclic order on a finite set as defined in 
Definition \ref{def:cyclic-order} is the same as a total cyclic order in the sense of Definition
\ref{def:totalcyclic}.
 
\item Let $\leq$ be a partial linear order on $S$. Its {\em cyclic closure} is the ternary relation
$\lambda=\lambda_\leq\subset S^3$ obtained as the closure of the set $\{x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3\}$ under
the action of $\mathbb{Z}/3$ by cyclic rotations. It is straightforward to see that $\lambda$ is a partial
cyclic order, total if $\leq$ is a total linear order, cf. \cite[Th. 3.5]{novak}.  

This implies that total cyclic order on a finite set $J$ with $|J|=n$ is the same as a class of
bijections $J\to \{1, 2, ..., n\}$  under the action of $\mathbb{Z}/n$, each bijection (i.e., a total
order) giving a cyclic order by cyclic closure. 

\item Every set $J$ has the {\em discrete partial cyclic order} consisting only of triples
	$(a,a,a)$, $a\in J$. If $|J|=1$, this is the only partial cyclic order on $J$.  If $|J|=2$,
	then $J$ has two partial cyclic orders: one discrete and the other is the total cyclic
	order, formed by all triples $(a,b,c)\in J^3$.  Note that Nov\'ak's setting \cite{novak}
	allows only one partial cyclic order on a 2-element set, the discrete one. 
	
	\item Generalizing (1), one can see that the set of points of any ``abstract circle"
	in the sense of Moerdijk \cite{moerdijk} has a total cyclic order.
	
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: The real projective line R P^1, being a circle, has a cyclic order. Such an order is determined by a choice of orientation of R^2. More generally, let F_n=Flag(1,2,...,n; R^n) be the space of complete flags in R^n. For example, F_2=R P^1. One of the main results of (theory of positive configurations of flags) says, in our terminology, that F_n has a natural partial cyclic order lambda, determined by a choice of orientation of R^n. Explicitly, a closed smooth curve Csubset R P^n-1 is called convex, if every hyperplane intersects C in at most n-1 points. In particular, such C does not lie in a hyperplane. Taking the osculating flags to C at all its points, we obtain an embedding gamma_C: Cto F_n. The 2-element set of orientations of any convex curve Csubset R P^n-1 is canonically identified with the 2-element set of orientations of R^n, by a version of the Frenet frame construction (this is the old-fashioned definition of the orientation of the space in terms of ``left and right screws"). Thus choosing an orientation of R^n, we equip any convex C with a total cyclic order lambda_C. We then say that (f_1, f_2, f_3)in F_n^3 lies in lambda, if there is a convex curve Cin R P^n-1 and three points (t_1, t_2, t_3)inlambda_C such that f_i=gamma_C(t_i). See loc. cit. for more details as well as a generalization to the complete flag variety of any split simple algebraic group over R.

nodes.statement: Let f: Ito J be a map of sets. Suppose that J is equipped with a partial cyclic order lambda_J, and each fiber f^-1(j) is equipped with a partial linear order leq_j. We say that (a,b,c)inlambda_I if (f(a), f(b), f(c))inlambda_J and either [labelindent=1cm] item[(i)] all three elements f(a), f(b), f(c) are distinct, or: item[(ii)] f(a)=f(b)neq f(c) and aleq_f(a) b, or: item[(ii')] f(a)=f(c)neq f(b) and cleq_f(c) a, or: item[(ii'')] f(a)neq f(b)=f(c) and bleq_f(b) c, or: item[(iii)] f(a)=f(b)=f(c) and either item aleq_j bleq_j c, or item bleq_j cleq_j a, or item cleq_j aleq_j b, \,\, j=f(a)=f(b)=f(c). nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defi:lexico} 
Let $f: I\to J$ be a map of sets.  Suppose that $J$ is equipped with a partial cyclic order
$\lambda_J$, and each fiber $f^{-1}(j)$ is equipped with a partial linear order $\leq_j$. In this
setting we construct a partial cyclic order $\lambda=\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))$ on $I$, called the {\em
lexicographic cyclic order} as follows. 
We say that $(a,b,c)\in\lambda_I$ if $(f(a), f(b), f(c))\in\lambda_J$ and either
\begin{enumerate}[labelindent=1cm]
\item[(i)]  all three elements $f(a), f(b), f(c)$  are distinct, or:

\item[(ii)]  $f(a)=f(b)\neq f(c)$ and $a\leq_{f(a)} b$,  or:

\item[(ii')] $f(a)=f(c)\neq f(b)$ and $c\leq_{f(c)}  a$, or:

\item[(ii'')] $f(a)\neq f(b)=f(c)$ and $b\leq_{f(b)} c$,  or:

\item[(iii)] $f(a)=f(b)=f(c)$ and either
\begin{enumerate}
\item $a\leq_j b\leq_j c$, or
\item $b\leq_j c\leq_j a$, or
\item $c\leq_j a\leq_j b$, \,\, $j=f(a)=f(b)=f(c)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
If $\lambda_J$ is a total cyclic order, and each $\leq_i$ is a total
linear order, then $\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))$ is a total cyclic order.

\label{def:morphisms-cyclic-orders}
 Let $(I,\lambda_I)$ and $(J, \lambda_J)$ be partially cyclically ordered sets. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),itemsep=0cm,topsep=1ex]
	\item Assume that $\lambda_I$ is a total cyclic order. Then we define a {\em morphism} $F: I\to J$
to be a datum consisting of a map $f: I\to J$ and a total linear order $\leq_j$ on
each $f^{-1}(j)$ such that $\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))=\lambda_I$.
	\item In general, a morphism $F: I\to J$ is a compatible system of
morphisms $I'\to J$ given for all totally cyclically ordered subsets $I'\subset I$  
(with respect to the induced cyclic order). 
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Let J subset S^1 be a subset of the standard circle. Providing J with the counter-clockwise cyclic order induced from S^1, we may identify the set Hom_Lambda(J, langle 0rangle) with the set of homotopy classes of monotone maps f: S^1 to S^1 of degree 1 taking the subset J to 1 in S^1. Let us refer to the arcs on S^1 which connect an element of J to its successor as interstices of J. The map f is uniquely determined by specifying which interstice of J maps to a nontrivial loop in S^1. Therefore, J^vee is canonically identified with the set of interstices of J subset S^1. For an abstract cyclically ordered set, the set J^vee should be regarded as an intrinsic construction of the set of interstices with its cyclic order, without any reference to an embedding into the circle. The role of J^vee as a dual object was emphasized by Drinfeld whose result can be formulated as follows.

nodes.statement: Although this is a particular case of the general duality for planar crossed simplicial groups, let us provide a self-contained proof for convenience of the reader. Given a morphism of cyclically ordered sets f: J to K, we obtain a map of sets of linear refinements f^vee: K^vee to J^vee. To lift this map to a morphism of cyclically ordered sets, we have to additionally provide a linear order on each fiber of f^vee. Consider linear orders lambda_1, lambda_2 in K^vee which map to the same linear order lambda in J^vee. Let j_max be the maximum of (J, lambda). We say lambda_1 le lambda_2 if \[ big|\k in K\; |\; f(j_max) le_lambda_1 k\big| le big|\k in K \;|\; f(j_max) le_lambda_2 k\big|. \] This construction provides linear orders on the fibers of f^vee which are compatible with the cyclic order on K^vee. The equivalence of categories can be verified by noting that the double dual (J^vee)^vee can be canonically and functorially identified with J.

nodes.statement: A dihedral order on a finite set J of cardinality ge 3 is defined to be the choice of a set o(J) = \lambda_0,lambda_1\ of opposite cyclic orders on J. A dihedral order on a set J of cardinality le 2 is defined to be the choice of an arbitrary two-element set o(J). Given a dihedrally ordered set (J, o(J)), we refer to the two-element set o(J) as the orientation torsor of J.

nodes.statement: (a) The reason for the introduction of a ``virtual'' orientation torsor for sets of cardinality le 2 should now be clear. For example, with this convention, the automorphism groups of the standard dihedrally ordered sets \0\ and \0,1\ are D_1 = Z/2 and D_2 = Z/2 times Z/2, respectively. The nontrivial automorphism given by interchanging the elements of the virtual orientation torsor acts trivially on the underlying sets. vskip .2cm (b) The automorphism of bf Lambda given by passing to the opposite cyclic order can be regarded as an action of the (discrete 2-) group Z/2 on bf Lambda. Our approach amounts to defining bfXi as the quotient of bfLambda by this action.

nodes.statement: item Every set of cardinality 1 le n le 2 admits a dihedral order which is unique up to nonunique isomorphism. This corresponds to the fact that we have surjections D_n to S_n with nontrivial kernel. Every set of cardinality 3 admits a unique dihedral order corresponding to the fact that we have an isomorphism D_3 to S_3. A set of cardinality n ge 3 has |S_n|/|D_n| different dihedral orders. item For a set J of cardinality ge 3, a dihedral order on J can be identified with an equivalence class of embeddings of J into the standard unit circle S^1 subset mathbb C. Here two embeddings are equivalent if they differ by a (not necessarily orientation preserving) homeomorphism of S^1. A set J of cardinality 4 has 3= |S_4|/|D_4| dihedral orders. These orders are in natural bijection with unordered partitions of J into two 2-element sets: J = \a,c\ sqcup \b,d\. This can be immediately seen by identifying a dihedral order with an equivalence class of embeddings into S^1: the above partition encodes that the diagonals [a,c] and [b,d] intersect inside the unit disk. \[ node (O) at (0,0) (origin) ; node (Pb) at (0:2cm) c; node (Pc) at (3.5*72:2cm) b; node (Pa) at (2.2*72:2cm) a; node (Pd) at (1*72:2cm) d; draw[ decoration=markings, postaction=decorate, dotted ] (origin) circle (2cm); draw (node cs:name=Pa) --(node cs:name=Pb); draw (node cs:name=Pc) --(node cs:name=Pd); \] Similarly, a dihedral order on a finite set J of cardinality geq 4 is uniquely determined by the knowledge of which pairs of diagonals intersect in the unit disk. In particular, this means that a dihedral order on J is uniquely recovered from the collection of the induced dihedral orders on all 4-element subsets of J. item Every finite cyclically ordered set (J, lambda) admits a canonical dihedral order by setting o(J) = \lambda, lambda^op\ if |J| ge 3 and o(J) = Z/2 otherwise. We call this dihedral order the dihedral closure of lambda. There is an obvious way to extend this construction to a faithful functor \[ Lambda longrightarrow Xi \] We denote the dihedral closure of the standard cyclically ordered set langle n rangle by overlinelangle n rangle. The small dihedral category Xi is then obtained as the full subcategory of Xi spanned by the standard dihedrally ordered sets \overlinelangle n rangle\.

nodes.statement: A more algebro-geometric version of Example can be obtained as follows. Let J be a finite set with geq 3 elements, and overline M_0,J be the moduli space of stable J-pointed curves of genus 0. This is a smooth projective variety over Q of dimension |J|-3 whose open part is the quotient \[ M_0,J = bigl( (P^1)^J setminus (diagonals )bigr) bigl/ PGL_2, \] see, e.g., for more details. Now note that connected components of the real locus M_0,J(R) are in bijection with dihedral orders on J. Indeed, R P^1= P^1(R) is topologically a circle, and action of PGL_2(R) on it contains transformations both preserving and reversing the orientation of this circle, so a comparison as in Example is immediate. It was proved in that the closure in overline M_0,J(R) of each component of M_0,J(R), is identified with the Stasheff polytope K_|J|-1. Thus overline M_0,J(R) can be obtained by gluing as many Stasheff polytopes as there are dihedral orders on J.
nodes.raw_latex:
A more algebro-geometric version of Example \ref{exa:dihedral} \ref{exa:item2} can be obtained
	as follows. Let  $J$ be a finite set with $\geq 3$ elements, and $\overline M_{0,J}$ be the
	moduli space of stable $J$-pointed curves of genus 0. This is a smooth projective  variety
	over $\mathbb{Q}$ of dimension $|J|-3$ whose open part is the quotient
	\[
	M_{0,J} = \bigl( (\mathbb{P}^1)^J \setminus (\text{diagonals} )\bigr) \bigl/ PGL_2,
	\]
	see, e.g., \cite{kapranov-veronese} for more details.  Now note that connected components of the
	real locus $M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ are in bijection with dihedral orders on $J$. Indeed, $\mathbb{R} P^1=
	\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{R})$ is topologically a circle, and action of $PGL_2(\mathbb{R})$ on it contains transformations
	both preserving and reversing the orientation of this circle, so a comparison as in 
	Example \ref{exa:dihedral} \eqref{exa:item2} is immediate. 
	It was proved in \cite{kapranov-permuto} that the closure in $\overline M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ of each component of
	$M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$, is identified with the Stasheff polytope $K_{|J|-1}$. Thus 
	$\overline M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ can be obtained by gluing as many Stasheff polytopes
	as there are dihedral orders on $J$.

Let $J$ be a finite dihedrally ordered set, $|J|\geq 5$, and $\gamma\subset J^4_\neq$
defined as above. For any ${\bf x}=(x_0, \dots, x_4) \in J^5_\neq$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] 
All $\partial_i {\bf x}$, $i=0, \dots, 4$, belong to $\gamma$.
In order words, the 
total order on $\{x_0, \dots, x_4\}$ is compatible with the induced cyclic order. 

\item[(ii)] $\partial_1{\bf x}$ and $\partial_3 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$.

\item[(iii)] $\partial_0{\bf x}$, $\partial_2{\bf x}$ and $\partial_4 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$. 
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Let J subset S^1 be a subset of the standard circle considered without chosen orientation. Then J inherits a natural dihedral order and the morphism set Hom_Xi(J, overline langle 0rangle) can be identified with homotopy classes of monotone homotopy equivalences f:S^1 to S^1 which map the subset J to the point 1 in S^1 where we orient the target circle counterclockwise. This map f is uniquely determined by the choice of an orientation and the choice of an interstice which maps to a nontrivial loop in S^1. Therefore, Hom_Xi(J, overline langle 0rangle) is in natural bijection with the set of oriented interstices of J subset S^1. The quotient set Hom_Xi(J, overline langle 0rangle)/(Z/2) is then identified with the set of unoriented interstices. The two possible choice of coherent orientations of all interstices correspond to the elements of the orientation torsor.

Let $J \subset S^1$ be a subset of the standard circle considered without chosen
	orientation. Then $J$ inherits a natural dihedral order and the morphism set
	$\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$ can be identified with homotopy classes of monotone homotopy
	equivalences $f:S^1 \to S^1$ which map the subset $J$ to the point $1 \in S^1$ where we
	orient the target circle counterclockwise. This map $f$ is uniquely determined by the choice
	of an orientation and the choice of an interstice which maps to a nontrivial loop in $S^1$.
	Therefore,  $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$ is in natural bijection with the set of {\em
	oriented interstices} of $J \subset S^1$. The quotient set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})/(\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is
	then identified with the set of {\em unoriented interstices}. The two possible choice of
	coherent orientations of all interstices correspond to the elements of the orientation torsor.

nodes.statement: A paracyclic order on a finite nonempty set J consists of item a Z-torsor widetildeJ, item a surjection pi: widetildeJ to J which exhibits J as the orbit set of the bijection \[T:\; widetildeJ to widetildeJ, widetildej mapsto widetildej + |J|.\]
nodes.raw_latex:
A {\em paracyclic order} on a finite nonempty set $J$ consists of 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor $\widetilde{J}$,
		\item a surjection $\pi: \widetilde{J} \to J$ which exhibits $J$ as the orbit set of
			the bijection \[T:\; \widetilde{J} \to \widetilde{J},\quad \widetilde{j} \mapsto \widetilde{j} +
				|J|.\]
	\end{enumerate}

\label{exa:paracyclic-exp}
Let $C$ be an oriented circle. A choice of a base point $c\in C$ defines a canonical 
paracyclic order on any finite nonempty $J\subset C$. More precisely, the choice of $c$
produces a canonical universal covering $\pi: \widetilde C_c\to C$, with $\widetilde C_c$ being
homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ and oriented, and so equipped with
a canonical total order. The discrete subset $\widetilde j=\pi^{-1}(J)$ has a natural successor operation 
induced by the  order on $\widetilde C_c$,  which makes it into a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor.
 The generator of the group $\mathbb{Z}$ of deck transformations
on $\widetilde C_c$ corresponds to the shift by $|J|$ in this torsor structure.

A {\em partial paracyclic order} on a set $J$ is a datum of:
\begin{enumerate}
