Let $J \subset S^1$ and consider the paracyclic order $\pi^{-1}(J) \to J$ on $J$ induced from the universal
	cover map $\pi: \mathbb{R} \to S^1$ (corresponding to the base point $1\in S^1$.
	 Then we can identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Lambda_{\infty}}(J, \operatorname{pt}\nolimits)$
	with homotopy classes of monotone maps $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ which 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item map the subset $\widetilde{J} \subset \mathbb{R}$ to the subset $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$, 
		\item are equivariant with respect to translation by $|J|$ on $\widetilde{J}$ and
			translation by $1$ on $\mathbb{Z}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Any such homotopy class is uniquely determined by specifying the interstice
	$[\widetilde{j},\widetilde{j}+1]$ of $\widetilde{J} \subset \mathbb{R}$ which maps
	onto the interstice $[0,1]$ of $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$. Thus the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}}$ can
	be naturally identified with the set of interstices of $\widetilde{J} \subset \mathbb{R}$. The
	quotient $J^{\vee}$ can therefore be canonically identified with the set of interstices of $J \subset
	S^1$.

nodes.raw_latex:
We give examples using the notation of Table \ref{table:corr}.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
		\item  For $G=O(2)$, we have $\mathbb{G}=GL(2,\mathbb{R})$, and a $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface is just a surface with no additional structure.

		\item For $G=SO(2)$, we have $\mathbb{G}=GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$, and a $\mathbb{G}$-structure on $S$ is the
			same as an orientation of $S$.

		\item For $G=\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$, the group $\mathbb{G}$ is the $N$-fold connected covering of $GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$, and
		a $\mathbb{G}$-structure is known as an $N$-{\em spin structure}.  The case $N=2$, being an instance
		of the spinor construction existing in any number of dimensions, has been studied more systematically, cf. \cite{johnson}. 

	\item For the unversal covering $G=\widetilde{SO(2)}$ of $SO(2)$, the group $\mathbb{G}=\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$
		is the universal covering of $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$. A $\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$-structure on a
		surface will be called a {\em framing}. Note that, in our definition, a framing on
		$S$ is a discrete datum: not an actual choice of a trivialization of $T_S$ but what
		amounts to an isotopy class of such trivializations. In fact, the same is true in
		all the other cases, and this is the reason for working with $\mathbb{G}$ instead of $G$.
		For instance, an $O(2)$-structure on $S$ is a Riemannian metric, while a
		$GL(2,\mathbb{R})$-structure is no extra structure at all. 
	\end{enumerate}

nodes.raw_latex:
Let $X$ be a topological space
and
\[
0\to A\longrightarrow\Gamma'\buildrel\pi\over\longrightarrow \Gamma\to 1
\]
be an extension of sheaves of groups on $X$ with abelian kernel $A$. Let $P$ be a sheaf of $\Gamma$-torsors
on $X$, with associated class $[P]\in H^1(X, \Gamma)$.
 In this situation, the $\Gamma$-action on $A$ by conjugation gives rise to the twisted form
$A^P$, a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ locally isomorphic to $A$. Denote by $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ the category
formed by sheaves $P'$ of $\Gamma'$-torsors on $X$ together with a $\pi$-equivariant 
map $\pi_{P'}: P'\to P$. Morphisms in $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ are isomorphisms of torsors
commuting with the projection to $P$. 
In the described situation, we have:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Each group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_{\operatorname{Lift}(P)}(P')$ is identified with $H^0(X, A^P)$.

\item[(ii)] The set of isomorphism classes of objects of $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ is either empty or is
a torsor over $H^1(X, A^P)$.

\item[(iii)] If $A$ is central, then there is a natural coboundary map of pointed sets
$\delta: H^1(X,\Gamma)\to H^2(X, A)$.
In this case $\operatorname{Lift}(P)\neq\emptyset$ if and only if $\delta([P])=0$. 
\end{enumerate}
Now, parts (a1-2) and (b1-2) follow by considering the extensions of sheaves
on $S$ obtained from \eqref{eq:group-K} by passing to sheaves of $C^\infty$-sections. Part (b3) follows from
Proposition \ref{prop:group-K}(b).

Let $S$ be a compact $C^\infty$-surface with boundary $\partial S$, and $S^\circ = S-\partial S$. 
The {\em Schottky double} of $S$ is the compact oriented $C^\infty$ surface $S^\#$
without boundary obtained by compatifying $\widetilde{S^\circ}$, the orientation cover of $S^\circ$,
by adding one copy of $\partial S$. Thus we have a 2-sheeted covering $\pi: S^\#\to S$, ramified
along $\partial S$, and the deck involution $\sigma: S^\#\to S^\#$ of this covering, reversing the
orientation and identical on  $\partial S$. If $(S,M)$ is a marked surface, we equip $S^\#$ with the
subset $M^\#=\pi^{-1}(M)$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
	\item An $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a {\em Riemann surface}, i.e., a
		1-dimensional complex manifold $X$ possibly with boundary. More precisely, an
		isomorphism class of objects of $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}} \operatorname{Str}(S)$ is the same as an almost
		complex structure $J: T_S\to T_S$, $J^2=-1$, and the automorphism group of any
		object of  $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}} \operatorname{Str}(S)$ is trivial. As well known, all almost complex
		structures in complex dimension $1$ are integrable. For a Riemann surface $X=(S,J)$
		we denote by $\overline X = (S, -J)$ the {\em conjugate} Riemann surface.

	\item  A $\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a triple $(X, \mathcal{L}, \phi)$
		where $X$ is a Riemann surface, $\mathcal{L}$ is a line bundle on $X$, and $\phi:
		\mathcal{L}^{\otimes N}\to\omega_X$ is an isomorphism. Here $\omega_X$ is the canonical line
		bundle of $X$.  For $N=2$, such line bundles $\mathcal{L}$ are traditionally called {\em
		theta-characteristics}, and a choice of $\mathcal{L}$ is often referred to as a ``spin
		structure" on $X$, cf.  \cite{atiyah}. For ``higher spin structures" on Riemann
		surfaces ($N>2$), see \cite{jarvis}. 
  
	\item An $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a {\em Klein surface}, i.e., a
		surface together with an atlas whose transition maps are conformal but do not
		necessarily preserve orientation.  Such maps are called {\em dianalytic} (i.e.,
		analytic or anti-analytic). Thus a Klein surface does not have to be orientable.
		See \cite{alling-greenleaf, braun} for more background. 
	\end{enumerate}

Let $g$ be the genus of $S$ and suppose that $(S,M)$ is stable, i.e., $2g-2+|M|>0$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ has a natural structure of a complex manifold of dimension $3g-3+|M|$. As
a $C^\infty$-manifold, it is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space. 

\item[(b)] Let $\sigma:S\to S$ be an orientation reversing involution preserving $M$ as a set. Conjugation
with $\sigma$ defines an anti-holomorphic involution
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{Teich}}: \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M). \qed
\]

\end{enumerate}

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:klein-teich}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $S$ is classical (i.e., orientable without boundary), then the space $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is the disjoint union of
two connected components, corresponding to the two orientations of $S$. Each component is canonically
identified with the corresponding classical Teichm\"uller space $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$. 

\item[(b1)] Suppose $S$ is non-classical, let $\pi: S^\#\to S$ be its Schottky double with involution
$\sigma$, and let $M^\#=\pi^{-1}(M)$. Let $g^\#$ be the genus of $S^\#$. Then
\[
\operatorname{Teich}(S,M) =  (\operatorname{Teich}^+(S^\#, M^\#))^{\sigma_{\operatorname{Teich}}}
\]
is the fixed point locus of the anti-holomorphic involution $\sigma_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. 
In particular, it is a real analytic manifold of dimension $3g^\#-3+|M^\#|$. 

\item[(b2)] Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, let $\varpi: \widetilde S\to S$ be its
orientation cover with the orientation reversing deck involution $\tau$, and let $\widetilde M=\varpi^{-1}(M)$.
Then
\[
	\operatorname{Teich}(S,M) = (\operatorname{Teich}^+(\widetilde S, \widetilde M))^{\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}}
\]
is the fixed point locus of the involution $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. 

\item[(c)] In the situation (b1), the manifold $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space.

\end{enumerate}

Let g^\# be the genus of S^\#. Then \[ Teich(S,M) = (Teich^+(S^\#, M^\#))^sigma_Teich \] is the fixed point locus of the anti-holomorphic involution sigma_Teich. Then \[ Teich(S,M) = (Teich^+(widetilde S, widetilde M))^tau_Teich \] is the fixed point locus of the involution tau_Teich. item[(c)] In the situation (b1), the manifold Teich(S,M) is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space.

nodes.statement: Let M be a finite set and suppose that 2g-2+|M|>0. Let M(g,M) be the Deligne-Mumford moduli stack formed by smooth projective algebraic curves X of genus g together with an embedding Mhookrightarrow X. Let (S,M) be a classical marked surface of genus g. Any choice of an orientation of S identifies M^SO(2)_conf_pure(S,M) with the groupoid (orbifold) of C-points M(g,M)(C). Change of orientation corresponds to the action of Gal(C/R) on M(g,M)(C) which comes from the fact that M(g,M) is defined over R (in fact, over Q). The orbifold M^SO(2)_conf is therefore the quotient of M(g,M)(C) by the symmetric group of M. As is well known, \[ M(g,M)(C) = Mod^+_pure(S,M) biglbackslash hskip -.1cm biglbackslash Teich^+(S,M) \] is the quotient of the topological cell Teich^+(S,M) by the mapping class group of orientation preserving diffeomorphisms fixing all points of M. In what follows, we realize a general M^G_conf(S,M) in terms of quotients of cells by discrete groups.

Let $M$ be a finite set and suppose that $2g-2+|M|>0$. Let $\mathcal{M}(g,M)$ be the Deligne-Mumford moduli stack
formed by smooth projective algebraic curves $X$ of genus $g$ together with an embedding $M\hookrightarrow X$. 
Let $(S,M)$ be a classical marked surface of genus $g$. Any choice of an orientation of $S$ identifies
$\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}_{{\operatorname{pure}}}(S,M)$ with the groupoid (orbifold) of $\mathbb{C}$-points $\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C})$. Change of orientation corresponds to the
action of $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R})$ on $\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C})$ which comes from the fact that $\mathcal{M}(g,M)$ is defined
over $\mathbb{R}$ (in fact, over $\mathbb{Q}$). The  orbifold $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is therefore the quotient of $\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C})$
by the symmetric group of $M$. As is well known,
\[
\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C}) = \operatorname{Mod}^+_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)
\]
is the quotient of the topological cell $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ by the mapping class group
of orientation preserving diffeomorphisms fixing all points of $M$. In what follows, we realize a general
$\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M)$ in terms of quotients of cells by discrete groups.

\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) & = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \bigl( \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ)) \times O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\bigr)\\
& = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \biggl\backslash \hskip -.25cm \biggl\backslash \coprod_{ \{F\}\in \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))} O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\\
& = \coprod _{ \{F\}\in \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))} \biggl( \operatorname{Stab}(F) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\biggr).
\end{align*}
Note that at the  bottom of last coproduct the quotient by $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$ is $\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$. At the same time,
$\operatorname{Stab}(F)$ is the union of connected components of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$, in particular,
$\operatorname{Stab}(F)_e = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)_e$. 
Therefore the above coproduct can be identified with
\[
\begin{gathered}
\coprod_{ \{F\}\in\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \pi_0 (\operatorname{Stab}(F)) 
\biggl\backslash \hskip -.25cm \biggl\backslash \biggl(  \operatorname{Stab}(F)_e \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\biggr)\,\,=
\\ =\,\,
\coprod_{ \{F\} \in\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S_F, M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}(S,M)
\end{gathered}
\]
as claimed. In the last identification, we identified the topological groupoid $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)$
with the topological space $\operatorname{Klein}(S)$ of its isomorphism classes. This is possible because
all automorphism groups of objects in this groupoid are trivial by Proposition 
\ref{prop:prod-of-grpds}(b).

nodes.name: graph
nodes.statement: A graph Gamma is a pair of sets (H,V) equipped with item an involution tau: H to H, item a map s: H to V. The elements of H are called halfedges of Gamma, the fixed points of tau are called external halfedges, and the nonfixed points of tau are called internal halfedges. The 2-element orbits of tau, which are hence comprised of a pair of internal halfedges, are called edges. The elements of V are called the vertices of Gamma. Given a vertex v in V, we define the set H(v) = s^-1(v) of halfedges incident to v. The cardinality |H(v)| is called the valency of v.
nodes.raw_latex:
A {\em graph} $\Gamma$ is a pair of sets $(H,V)$ equipped with
\begin{itemize}
	\item an involution $\tau: H \to H$,
	\item a map $s: H \to V$.
\end{itemize}
The elements of $H$ are called {\em halfedges} of $\Gamma$, the fixed points of $\tau$ are called
{\em external halfedges}, and the nonfixed points of $\tau$ are called {\em internal halfedges}. 
The $2$-element orbits of $\tau$, which are hence comprised of a pair of internal halfedges, are called {\em edges}. 
The elements of $V$ are called the {\em vertices} of $\Gamma$.  Given a vertex $v \in V$, we define the set $H(v) =
s^{-1}(v)$ of {\em halfedges incident to $v$}. The cardinality $|H(v)|$ is called the valency of
$v$.
nodes.clean_text: A graph Gamma is a pair of sets (H,V) equipped with item an involution tau: H to H, item a map s: H to V. The elements of H are called halfedges of Gamma, the fixed points of tau are called external halfedges, and the nonfixed points of tau are called internal halfedges. The 2-element orbits of tau, which are hence comprised of a pair of internal halfedges, are called edges. The elements of V are called the vertices of Gamma. Given a vertex v in V, we define the set H(v) = s^-1(v) of halfedges incident to v. The cardinality |H(v)| is called the valency of v.

nodes.name: incidence diagram of $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Let Gamma be a graph. The incidence category I(Gamma) of Gamma has, as objects, all the vertices and edges of Gamma with a non-identity morphism s(h) to \h,tau(h)\ for every internal halfedge h. The incidence diagram of Gamma is the functor \[ I_Gamma: I(Gamma) longrightarrow mathcal Set \] given on objects by assigning to a vertex v the set H(v) and to an edge e with half-edges h,h', the 2-element set \h,h'\. To a morphism s(h) to \h,h'\ we associate the map of sets H(s(h)) to \h,h'\ given by mapping h to h' and collapsing the remaining halfedges in H(s(h)) (denoted by A in Fig. ) to h.

Let $\Gamma$ be a graph. The {\em incidence category} $I(\Gamma)$ of $\Gamma$ has, as objects,
all the vertices and edges of $\Gamma$ with a non-identity morphism $s(h) \to
\{h,\tau(h)\}$ for every internal halfedge $h$. The {\em incidence diagram of $\Gamma$} is the functor
\[
	I_{\Gamma}: I(\Gamma) \longrightarrow {\mathcal Set}
\]
given on objects by assigning to a vertex $v$ the set $H(v)$ and to an edge $e$ with half-edges $h,h'$,  the
$2$-element set  $\{h,h'\}$. To a morphism $s(h) \to \{h,h'\}$ we associate the map of sets
$H(s(h)) \to \{h,h'\}$ given by mapping $h$ to $h'$ and collapsing the remaining halfedges in
$H(s(h))$  (denoted by A in Fig. \ref{fig:F1}) to $h$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defi:exggraphs}  
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item A graph with a $\Lambda$-structure is called a {\em ribbon graph}.
		Explicitly, a $\Lambda$-structure on a graph $\Gamma$ is the datum of a cyclic order
		on the $H(v)$ for each vertex $v\in V$. Each  set $\{h,h'\}$ of half-edges of any edge $e$
		has a trivial cyclic order, since it has cardinality 2. 
		Thus, our definition reduces to the usual one
		\cite{penner:book}. 
		
		\item A graph with a $\Xi$-structure is called a {\em M\"obius graph}.
		Explicitly, a $\Xi$-structure on a graph $\Gamma$  consists,
		first, of a dihedral order on each $H(v)$ and, second, of identification
		of the orientation torsors 
		\[
		O(H(v))\buildrel\sim\over \longleftarrow O(e)\buildrel\sim\over \longrightarrow O(H(v'))
		\]
		for each edge $e$ with vertices
		$v$ and $v'$ (the case $v=v'$ is allowed).
		 This structure  
		is equivalent to the (somewhat more cumbersome)  concept of a M\"obius graph defined
		 in terms of ``ribbon graphs with  $\mathbb{Z}/2$-grading
		on edges" as in \cite{braun, mulase-waldron, mulase-yu}.  
								
		\item A graph with a $\Lambda_{\infty}$-structure is called a {\em framed graph}.
		\item A graph with a $\Lambda_N$-structure is called an {\em $N$-spin graph}.
		Very recently, surfaces with 2-spin structure were studied, from a combinatorial point of
		view by Novak and Runkel \cite{novak-runkel}. They introduced a concept of
		a combinatorial spin structure on a triangulation $T$ of a surface $S$. Such a structure
		equips the dual graph of $T$ with a $\Lambda_2$-structure in our sense. 
	\end{enumerate}

A G-structure on S gives, via the homotopy equivalence Gto Homeo^G(S^1), a Homeo^G(S^1)-structure on each circle C(T_xS). Therefore, by Corollary , each finite subset of C(T_xS) becomes, canonically, a Delta G-structured set. In particular, for each vertex v in V, we have a canonical embedding of sets H(v)hookrightarrow C(T_gamma(v) S) given by association to a half-edge h the direction given by the germ of the path gamma(|h|) leaving v. By the above, this provides a canonical Delta G-structure on the set H(v). Further, let e be an edge of Gamma given by a pair of half-edges h, h' as above. The two tangent directions to |Gamma| at gamma(m(e)) correspond to the two half-edges h and h' of e. As before, the embedding |Gamma|to S gives a Delta G-structure on the 2-element set of these directions, i.e., on \h,h'\. This defines the values of the functor widetilde I_Gamma: I(Gamma)to G on objects. \begin{enumerate}
	\item Suppose ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}=\Lambda$. If $\Gamma$ be embedded into an oriented surface $S$, then it is classical that $\Gamma$
		is canonically a ribbon graph. Explicitly, each $H(v)$ has a cyclic order from the embedding
		into the oriented circle $C(T_{\gamma(v)} S)$, while the set of half-edges of any edge
		has a unique cyclic order since it has cardinality $2$. 
			
	\item Suppose ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}=\Xi$.
		 Let $\Gamma$ be embedded into an unoriented surface $S$. Then $\Gamma$
		naturally admits the structure of a M\"obius graph.  The set 		$H(v)$ of half-edges incident to $v$
		inherits a dihedral order from the embedding into the circle $C(T_{\gamma(v)} S)$.
		The set $\{h,h'\}$ of half-edges of an edge $e$ is made into a dihedral set by looking at
		the orientation cover $\varpi: \widetilde \to S$: we define the orientation torsor $O(\{h,h'\})$
		of this set to be the set of sections of $\pi$ over the image, under $\gamma$, of the interior of $|e|$. 
		 Finally, we have to provide a lift of 
		the incidence map $i: H(s(h)) \to \{h,h'\}$ to a morphism of dihedrally ordered
		sets. Note that, by the path lifting property of the orientation cover $\pi$, 
		the orientation torsors of $H(s(h))$ and $\{h,h'\}$ are canonically
		identified. For every choice of orientation, there is now a unique linear
		order on $i^{-1}(h')$ compatible with the corresponding cyclic order of
		$H(s(h))$. These two linear orders are opposite providing $i$ with the
		structure of a morphism in ${\Xi}$.
			
	\item  Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}={\Lambda}_\infty$. 
		Assume that $\Gamma$ is embedded into a framed surface $S$. This means, in
		particular, that $S$ is oriented so that we have a principal $GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$-bundle $\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$ of positive frames on $S$. 
		Further, we are given a principal $\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$-bundle $\widetilde\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$ covering $\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$. 
		Thus, each fiber of $\widetilde\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$ is a universal cover of the corresponding fiber of $\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$.
		Let
		\[
		B^+ \,\,=\,\, \biggl\{
		\begin{pmatrix}
		a&b\\0&c
		\end{pmatrix}\,\in GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})\bigl\| \,\, a,c >0\biggr\}. 
		\]
		Then $B^+\backslash GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})=S^1$ is the circle of directions of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Therefore 
		$B^+\backslash \operatorname{Fr}^+_S=C(T_S)$ is the circle bundle of directions of $T_S$. Further, $B^+$, being
		contractible, lifts canonically to a subgroup $\widetilde B^+\subset\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$.
		The quotient $\widetilde B^+\backslash \widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}\simeq\mathbb{R}$ is the universal covering of
		$S^1$. So each fiber $\widetilde C(T_xS)= \widetilde B^+\backslash \widetilde\operatorname{Fr}^+_{S,x}$ is an oriented
		real line, equipped with the projection $\pi_x: \widetilde C(T_xS)\to C(T_xS)$
		exhibiting it as a universal covering of $C(T_xS)$. Therefore, for each vertex $v\in\Gamma$
		the preimage of $H(v)\subset C(T_{\gamma(v)}S)$ is naturally a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor, thus giving a paracyclic
		order on $H(v)$. Similarly for each edge $\{h,h'\}$. We leave remaining details to the reader. 
		
	\item  Assume that $\Gamma$ is embedded into a surface $S$ which has an $N$-spin
		structure. Then, similarly to (3) , we consider an $N$-fold covering 
		$\pi_x: \widetilde C_N(T_xS)\to C(T_xS)$ for each $x\in S$. Taking $\pi_{\gamma(v)}^{-1}(H(v))$,
		we make each $H(v)$ into an $N$-cyclic set, and similarly for each set $\{h,h'\}$. 
\end{enumerate}

Let $(S,M)$ be a stable marked surface. A {\em spanning graph} for $(S,M)$
is a graph $\Gamma$ together with an embedding $\gamma: |\Gamma|\to S$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\gamma$ is a homotopy equivalence.
\item The restriction of $\gamma$ defines a homotopy equivalence between $\partial |\Gamma|$
(a finite set of points) and $\partial S - M$ (a finite set of open intervals). 
\end{enumerate}
We define the category $P(S,M)$ whose objects are isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$ and
with a unique morphism $[\Gamma] \to [\Gamma']$ if $[\Gamma']$ is obtained from $[\Gamma]$
by collapsing a forest. Note that $P(S,M)$ is in fact a poset.

\label{prop:Gc-operad} Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a crossed simplicial group.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item The action of $S_n$ on $P_\mathcal{G}(n)$ by relabelling the incoming external halfedges and
		the maps $\{ m_{a_1, \dots, a_n} \}$ make $P_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}= \{P_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ an operad in the
		category of sets. 
	\item Assume that ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is planar. Then algebras over $P_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ are precisely monoids with a
		twisted action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ in the sense of \S \ref{section:semiconstant}.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Part (1) is clear. We show (2). Given an augmented Delta G-structured tree Gamma in Tr_Delta G(n) with augmented incidence diagram I(Gamma) to mathcal G, we first argue that we can contract all internal edges to obtain a corolla. To this end, we note that, given an internal edge \e,e'\ incident to vertices v and v', the corresponding diagram \[ H(v) longrightarrow \e,e'\ longleftarrow H(v') \] has a limit in mathcal G whose underlying set is given by (H(v)setminus \e\) cup (H(v') setminus \e'\). This holds for all planar crossed simplicial groups and can be verified using the topological model of Delta G from S . We can use the cone diagram of this limit in mathcal G to produce a morphism of Delta G-structured graphs Gamma to Gamma' which collapses the edge \e,e'\. After collapsing all internal edges of Gamma, we obtain an augmented Delta G-structured n-corolla Gamma_0. Using the labels we can identify the set H(v) of halfedges incident to the single vertex of Gamma_0 with \0,1,dots,n\. We can find an isomorphism of Delta G-structured sets f: (\0,1,dots,n\, mathcal O) cong [n] and since, for planar crossed simplicial groups, G_n acts (simply) transitively on Hom_Delta G([0],[n]) we may assume that f maps 0 to 0. Therefore, after permuting the labels 1,2, dots, n, we may assume that H(v) = [n]. Every morphism [n] to [1] such that varphi^-1(0) = \0\ (corresponding to the outgoing halfedge labeled 0) can be written as a composite varphi g where varphi: [n] to [1] is the morphism in Delta which maps 0 to 0 and all remaining elements to 1, and g in Stab(0) subset G_n. Therefore, we can assume that the augmentation H(v) = [n] to [1] of the single outgoing halfedge 0 is given by varphi. For every 1 le i le n, the subset of Hom_Delta G([n],[1]) given by those morphisms such that varphi^-1(1) = \i\ forms a torsor under the action of G_1^0 cong G_0. Note that this action of G_0 is precisely the operadic action of the monoid P_Delta G(1) on the incoming halfedges. Therefore, the collection of isomorphism classes of labelled augmented Delta G-structured n-corollas forms a torsor under the action of \[ underbraceP_Delta G(1) times P_Delta G(1) times dots times P_Delta G(1)_n times S_n. \] We will now trivialize this torsor, for every n, by choosing a specific Delta G-structured n-corolla in such a way that these chosen n-corollas are closed under operadic composition (for n>1). To this end, choose a duality functor D: Delta G to Delta G^op and consider the diagram \[ xymatrix [1] ar[drr]_\0,1\& [1] ar[dr]^\1,2\ & dots & [1] ar[dl]^\n-1,n\\\ & & [n] & \\ & & [1]ar[u]^\0,n\ & \] in Delta subset Delta G and apply D to obtain the incidence diagram of a labeled augmented Delta G-structured n-corolla which we define to be our chosen trivialization. It is easy to verify that, due to the functoriality of D, the collection of corollas thus obtained is closed under operadic composition. This exhibits a copy of the associative operad Ass in P such that every element of P can be uniquely expressed as an element of Ass precomposed with elements of the monoid P_Delta G(1) acting on the incoming halfedges. An explicit computation of the action of P_Delta G(1) on the outgoing halfedges of Ass in terms of the actions on the incoming halfedges implies the claim that P parametrizes algebras with twisted G_0-action.

Part (1) is clear. We show (2). Given an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured tree $\Gamma$ in
	$\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ with augmented incidence diagram $I(\Gamma) \to {\mathcal G}$, we first argue that we
	can contract all internal edges to obtain a corolla. To this end, we note that, given an
	internal edge $\{e,e'\}$ incident to vertices $v$ and $v'$, the corresponding diagram
	\[
		H(v) \longrightarrow \{e,e'\} \longleftarrow H(v') 
	\]
	has a limit in ${\mathcal G}$ whose underlying set is given by $(H(v)\setminus \{e\}) \cup (H(v')
	\setminus \{e'\})$. This holds for all planar crossed simplicial groups and can be 
	verified using the topological model of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ from \S \ref{sec:topmodel}.
	We can use the cone diagram of this limit in ${\mathcal G}$ to produce a morphism of
	${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma \to \Gamma'$ which collapses the edge $\{e,e'\}$. After
	collapsing all internal edges of $\Gamma$, we obtain an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured 
	$n$-corolla $\Gamma_0$. Using the labels we can identify the set $H(v)$ of halfedges
	incident to the single vertex of $\Gamma_0$ with $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. We can find an
	isomorphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $f: (\{0,1,\dots,n\}, {\mathcal O}) \cong [n]$ and since, for planar
	crossed simplicial groups, $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts (simply) transitively on $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([0],[n])$ we
	may assume that $f$ maps $0$ to $0$. Therefore, after permuting the labels $1,2, \dots, n$,
	we may assume that $H(v) = [n]$. Every morphism $[n] \to [1]$ such that $\varphi^{-1}(0) =
	\{0\}$ (corresponding to the outgoing halfedge labeled $0$) can be written as a composite 
	$\varphi g$ where $\varphi: [n] \to [1]$ is the morphism in $\Delta$ which maps $0$ to $0$
	and all remaining elements to $1$, and $g \in \operatorname{Stab}(0)
	\subset \mathfrak{G}_n$. Therefore, we can assume that the augmentation $H(v) = [n] \to [1]$ of the
	single outgoing halfedge $0$ is given by $\varphi$. 
	For every $1 \le i \le n$, the subset of $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([n],[1])$ given by those morphisms such
	that $\varphi^{-1}(1) = \{i\}$ forms a torsor under the action of $\mathfrak{G}_1^0 \cong \mathfrak{G}_0$. 
	Note that this action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ is precisely the operadic action of the monoid
	$P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ on the incoming halfedges. Therefore, the collection of isomorphism classes of
	labelled augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corollas forms a torsor under the action of 
	\[
		\underbrace{P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1) \times P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1) \times \dots \times P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)}_n \times S_{n}.
	\]
	We will now trivialize this torsor, for every $n$, by choosing a specific ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured
	$n$-corolla in such a way that these chosen $n$-corollas are closed under operadic
	composition (for $n>1$). To this end, choose a duality functor $D: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ and consider the
	diagram
	\[
		\xymatrix{ [1] \ar[drr]_{\{0,1\}}& [1] \ar[dr]^{\{1,2\}} & \dots & [1] \ar[dl]^{\{n-1,n\}}\\
			& & [n] & \\
			& & [1]\ar[u]^{\{0,n\}} & 
		}
	\]
	in $\Delta \subset {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ and apply $D$ to obtain the incidence diagram of a labeled augmented
	${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla which we define to be our chosen trivialization. It is easy to
	verify that, due to the functoriality of $D$, the collection of corollas thus obtained is
	closed under operadic composition. This exhibits a copy of the associative operad $\operatorname{Ass}$
	in $P$ such that every element of $P$ can be uniquely expressed as an element of $\operatorname{Ass}$
	precomposed with elements of the monoid $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ acting on the incoming halfedges. An
	explicit computation of the action of $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ on the outgoing halfedges of $\operatorname{Ass}$
	in terms of the actions on the incoming halfedges implies the claim that $P$ parametrizes
	algebras with twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action.

nodes.name: orbicell decomposition
nodes.statement: Let X be a topological groupoid. An orbicell decomposition of X is a finite filtration \[ X = bigl( X_0subsetX_1 subsetcdotssubset X_n = X) \] of X by closed topological subgroupoids X_d such that: item[(1)] Each X_d is a full subcategory in X. item[(2)] Each component of X_d-X_d-1 is a disjoint union of d-orbicells.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $X$ be a topological groupoid. An {\em orbicell decomposition} of $X$ is a finite filtration
   \[
   \mathcal{X} = \bigl( \mathcal{X}_0\subset\mathcal{X}_1 \subset\cdots\subset \mathcal{X}_n = X)
   \]
   of $X$ by closed topological subgroupoids $\mathcal{X}_d$ such that:
   \begin{enumerate}
   \item[(1)] Each $\mathcal{X}_d$ is a full subcategory in $X$.
   
   \item[(2)] Each component of $\mathcal{X}_d-\mathcal{X}_{d-1}$ is a disjoint union of $d$-orbicells.
   \end{enumerate}

\label{ex:regular-cell}
  Let $Y$ be a topological space with a cell decomposition ${\mathcal Y}$. Let $D$ be a discrete
  group acting on $Y$, preserving ${\mathcal Y}$ and such that for each cell $\sigma$ of ${\mathcal Y}$ the stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}(\sigma)$
 acting on $\sigma$, makes $\operatorname{Stab}(\sigma)\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash\sigma$ into an orbicell. Then the groupoid
 $D\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash Y$ has an orbicell decomposition into orbicells $\operatorname{Stab}(\sigma)\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash\sigma$ where $\sigma$ runs
 over orbits of $D$ on the set of cells of ${\mathcal Y}$.

nodes.statement: underbar(a) Oriented case G=SO(2). In this case, the statement (that the usual moduli space of stable marked Riemann surfaces has an orbicell decomposition labelled by ribbon graphs) is well known, see, e.g., and references therein. We indicate here the main steps which we later analyze to deduce the general case. First, each component of M^SO(2)_conf is a quotient groupoid \[ M^SO(2)_conf(S,M) \,\,=\,\, Mod^+(S,M)biglbackslash hskip -.1cm biglbackslashTeich^+(S,M). \] Second, Teich^+(S,M) has a Mod^+(S,M)-invariant regular cell decomposition (triangulation) constructed by Harer and described in Appendix . Denote this cell decomposition by mathcal Y. The simplices of mathcal Y correspond to tesselations of (S,M) or, dually, to isotopy classes of spanning graphs for (S,M). Inclusions of simplices correspond to coarsenings of tesselations or, dually, to contractions of spanning graphs. Any spanning graph for (S,M) carries an induced ribbon structure. Therefore, orbicells in the quotient orbicell decomposition, which we denote X_S,M, form a full subcategory in Lambda-Graph with objects those graphs that appear as spanning graphs for (S,M). Finally, each ribbon graph Gamma gives rise to an oriented marked surface (S,M) obtained by ``thickening" Gamma, so that Gamma becomes a spanning graph for (S,M), see, e.g., S 3.3.4. This shows that for X=coprod_(S,M) X_S,M, we have Cell(X)simeq Lambda-Graph. Note that Costello introduced another topological groupoid N with an orbicell decomposition labelled by Lambda-Graph which is homotopy equivalent, but not homeomorphic to M^SO(2)_conf. vskip .3cm underbar(b) Unoriented case G=O(2). It is treated similarly to the oriented case, using the identification \[ M^O(2)_conf(S,M) \,\,=\,\,Mod(S,M) biglbackslash hskip -.1cm biglbackslash Teich(S,M) \] and the triangulation mathcal Y of Teich(S,M) described in S . As before, the simplices of mathcal Y correspond to triangulations of (S,M) and give M\"obius graphs as Mod(S,M)-orbits. Further, any M\"obius graph Gamma can be ``thickened" producing an unoriented surface (S,M) in which it is spanning. So, for the resulting quotient orbicell decomposition X of M^O(2)_conf we have Cell(X)simeq Xi-Graph. Note that an analog of Costello's approach for Klein surfaces was developed by Braun . vskip .3cm underbar(c) General case: G an arbitrary planar Lie group. Depending on whether G preserves orientation or not, we consider one of the two projections \[ pi: M^G_conf longrightarrow M^SO(2)_conf, pi: M^G_conf longrightarrow M^O(2)_conf \] obtained by forgetting the extra structure. In each case, the projection pi is an unramified covering of orbifolds, so the preimage of any orbicell in the target is a disjoint union of orbicells in the source. We thus obtain an orbicell decomposition of M^G_conf which we now analyze. We sketch the case when G does not preserve the orientation, the other case being similar but easier. Denote by X the orbicell decomposition of M^O(2)_conf and by X^G the preimage decomposition of M^G_conf. Since any G_conf-structured marked surface is G-structured, any tessellation P of the surface makes the dual graph of P into a Delta G-structured graph. We obtain therefore a commutative diagram of categories \[ xymatrix Cell(X^G) ar[d]_q_G ar[r]^pi & Cell(X) ar[d]^q \\ Delta G-Graph ar[r]_varpi & Xi-Graph \] where q is an equivalence by the case (b) above. We prove that q_G is an equivalence as well. For this, we note that any morphism Gamma to Gamma' in Delta G-Graph can be expressed uniquely as the composition of a contraction of a set of I of edges of Gamma (which results in a canonical contraction morphism Gamma to Gamma_I) followed by an isomorphism Gamma_I to Gamma'. This implies that, assuming Hom_Delta G-Graph(Gamma,Gamma') ne emptyset, any fiber of the map \[ Hom_Delta G-Graph(Gamma,Gamma') longrightarrow Hom_Xi-Graph(varpi(Gamma),varpi(Gamma')) \] is acted upon simply transitively by the group Autnolimits(Gamma'/varpi(Gamma')) of automorphisms of Gamma' which induce the identity on varpi(Gamma'). A similar analysis of the morphisms in Cell(X^G) implies that the fibers of the map \[ Hom_Cell(X^G)(sigma,sigma') longrightarrow Hom_Cell(X)(pi(sigma),pi(sigma')) \] are torsors for the group Autnolimits(sigma'/pi(sigma')) of automorphisms of sigma' inducing the identity on pi(sigma'). Since we already know that the map q is fully faithful, to show that q^G is fully faithful, it therefore suffices to show that the induced map \[ Autnolimits(sigma'/pi(sigma')) longrightarrow Autnolimits(q^G(sigma')/q^G(pi(sigma'))) \] is bijective. Showing this statement and the essential surjectivity of q^G amounts to showing that q^G induces an equivalence of all strict fiber categories of pi and varpi. This is shown in the following lemma.
nodes.raw_latex:
\underbar{(a) Oriented case } $G=SO(2)$. In this case, the statement (that the usual
	moduli space of stable marked {\em Riemann surfaces} has an orbicell decomposition labelled
	by ribbon graphs) is well known, see, e.g., \cite{arbarello, penner:book} and references
	therein. We indicate here the main steps which we later analyze to deduce the general case.
 
	First, each component of $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is a quotient groupoid 
	\[
	 \mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Mod}^+(S,M)\bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M).
	\]
	Second, $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$  has a $\operatorname{Mod}^+(S,M)$-invariant regular cell decomposition
	(triangulation)  constructed by Harer \cite{harer} and described in Appendix \ref
	{subsub:harer}.  Denote this cell decomposition by ${\mathcal Y}$.  The simplices of ${\mathcal Y}$ correspond
	to tesselations of $(S,M)$ or, dually, to isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$.
	Inclusions of simplices correspond to coarsenings of tesselations or, dually, to contractions of
	spanning graphs.  Any spanning graph for $(S,M)$ carries an induced ribbon structure.
	Therefore, orbicells in the quotient orbicell decomposition, which we denote $\mathcal{X}_{S,M}$,
	form a full subcategory in $\Lambda-\operatorname{Graph}$ with objects those graphs that appear as
	spanning graphs for $(S,M)$.  Finally, each ribbon graph $\Gamma$ gives rise to an oriented
	marked surface $(S,M)$ obtained by ``thickening" $\Gamma$, so that $\Gamma$ becomes a
	spanning graph for $(S,M)$, see, e.g., \cite{HSS-triangulated} \S 3.3.4. This shows that for
	$\mathcal{X}=\coprod_{(S,M)} \mathcal{X}_{S,M}$, we have ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq {\Lambda}-\operatorname{Graph}$. 

	Note that Costello \cite{costello-dual} introduced another topological groupoid $\mathcal{N}$ with
	an orbicell decomposition labelled by ${\Lambda}-\operatorname{Graph}$ which is homotopy equivalent,
	but not homeomorphic to $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$. 

	\vskip .3cm

	\underbar{(b) Unoriented case} $G=O(2)$. It is treated similarly to the oriented case, using
	the identification \[ \mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\,\operatorname{Mod}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) \] and the
	triangulation ${\mathcal Y}$ of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ described in \S \ref{subsub:harer}. As before, the
	simplices of ${\mathcal Y}$ correspond to triangulations of $(S,M)$ and give M\"obius graphs as
	$\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-orbits. Further, any M\"obius graph $\Gamma$ can be ``thickened" producing an
	unoriented surface $(S,M)$ in which it is spanning. So, for the resulting quotient orbicell
	decomposition $\mathcal{X}$ of $\mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ we have ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq {\Xi}-\operatorname{Graph}$. 

	Note that an analog of Costello's approach \cite{costello-dual} for Klein surfaces was developed
	by Braun \cite{braun}. 

	\vskip .3cm

	\underbar{(c) General case:} $G$ an arbitrary planar Lie group. Depending on whether $G$
	preserves orientation or not, we consider one of the two projections
	\[
	\pi: \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}, \quad  \pi: \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}
	\]
	obtained by forgetting the extra structure. In each case, the projection $\pi$ is an
	unramified covering of orbifolds, so the preimage of any orbicell in the target is a
	disjoint union of orbicells in the source.  We thus obtain an orbicell decomposition of
	$\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ which we now analyze. We sketch the case when $G$ does not preserve the
	orientation, the other case being similar but easier. 
	Denote by $\mathcal{X}$ the orbicell decomposition of $\mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ and by $\mathcal{X}^G$ the preimage
	decomposition of $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}$. Since any $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured marked surface is
	$\mathbb{G}$-structured, any tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of the surface makes the dual graph of $\mathcal{P}$ into
	a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph. We obtain therefore a commutative diagram of categories
	\[
	\xymatrix{
	{\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X}^G)
	\ar[d]_{q_G} \ar[r]^{\pi} & {\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})
	\ar[d]^q
	\\
	{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \ar[r]_\varpi & {\Xi}-\operatorname{Graph}
	}
	\]
	where $q$ is an equivalence by the case (b) above. We prove that $q_G$ is an equivalence as well.
	For this, we note that any morphism $\Gamma \to \Gamma'$ in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}$ can be expressed
	uniquely as the composition of a contraction of a set of $I$ of edges of $\Gamma$ (which
	results in a canonical contraction morphism $\Gamma \to \Gamma_I$) followed by an isomorphism 
	$\Gamma_I \to \Gamma'$. This implies that, assuming $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}}(\Gamma,\Gamma') \ne
	\emptyset$, any
	fiber of the map 
	\[
		\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}}(\Gamma,\Gamma') \longrightarrow
		\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Xi}-\operatorname{Graph}}(\varpi(\Gamma),\varpi(\Gamma'))
	\]
	is acted upon simply transitively by the group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(\Gamma'/\varpi(\Gamma'))$ of automorphisms of $\Gamma'$ which induce
	the identity on $\varpi(\Gamma')$. A similar analysis of the morphisms in ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X}^G)$
	implies that the fibers of the map 
	\[
		\operatorname{Hom}_{{\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X}^G)}(\sigma,\sigma') \longrightarrow
		\operatorname{Hom}_{{\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})}(\pi(\sigma),\pi(\sigma'))
	\]
	are torsors for the group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(\sigma'/\pi(\sigma'))$ of automorphisms of $\sigma'$
	inducing the identity on $\pi(\sigma')$.
	Since we already know that the map $q$ is fully faithful, to show that $q^G$ is fully
	faithful, it therefore suffices to show that the induced map 
	\[
		\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(\sigma'/\pi(\sigma')) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(q^G(\sigma')/q^G(\pi(\sigma')))
	\]
	is bijective. Showing this statement and the essential surjectivity of $q^G$ amounts to  
	showing that $q^G$ induces an equivalence of all strict fiber categories of $\pi$ and
	$\varpi$. This is shown in the following lemma.

nodes.statement: We first show that q_Gamma is essentially surjective. Let F_Gamma be a Delta G-structure on Gamma. By Theorem , F_Gamma can be seen as a datum, for each xinGammasubset S', of a Homeo^G(S^1)-structure on the circle of directions C_x(S). Moreover, these structures are compatible as x moves in Gamma, thus providing a Homeo^G(S^1)-structure on C(T_S)|_Gamma, the restriction to Gamma of the circle bundle C(T_S). Since Gamma is homotopy equivalent to S-M and hence to S-(Mcap S^circ), we get a unique, up to isomorphism, Homeo^G(S^1)-structure on C(T_S-(Mcap S^circ)). Finally, since Gto Homeo^G(S^1) is a homotopy equivalence, we obtain from this a G-structure on S-(Mcap S^circ). Thus q_Gamma is essentially surjective. Second, we show that q_Gamma induces bijections on Hom-sets. Because GStr(S) is a groupoid, it is enough to show that for each G-structure F on S-(Mcap S^circ) the induced map of automorphism groups \[ q_*: Autnolimits(F)longrightarrowAutnolimits(F_Gamma) \] is an isomorphism. Note that q_* actually comes (by passing to global sections) from a homomorphism of sheaves of groups on Gamma formed by local isomorphisms: \[ underline q_*: underline Autnolimits(F)longrightarrowunderline Autnolimits(F_Gamma). \] So it is enough to prove that underline q_*: is an isomorphism of sheaves. By Proposition (b1), underlineAutnolimits(F)=underline K^or is the local system obtained by the orientation twist of K=Kernolimits\Gto GL(2,R)\. Now note that K can also be identified with Kernolimits\G_nto D_n+1\ for any n by Theorem (b2). An automorphism of the Delta G-structure F_Gamma (identical on Gamma) is therefore a section of a local system L on Gamma whose stalk at each point is isomorphic to K. The final identification of L with underline K^or and of q_* with the identity of underline K^or is left to the reader.

	 Second, we show that $q_\Gamma$ induces bijections on Hom-sets. Because $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S)$ is a
	 groupoid, it is enough to show that for each $\mathbb{G}$-structure $F$ on $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$ the
	 induced map of automorphism groups
	 \[
		 q_*: \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F_\Gamma)
	 \]
	 is an isomorphism. Note that $q_*$ actually comes (by passing to global sections) from a
	 homomorphism of sheaves of groups on $\Gamma$ formed by local isomorphisms:
	 \[
		  \underline q_*: \underline \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F)\longrightarrow\underline \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F_\Gamma). 
	 \]
	 So it is enough to prove that $  \underline q_*:$ is an isomorphism of sheaves. By
	 Proposition \ref{prop:G-structures}(b1), $\underline\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F)=\underline K^{\operatorname{or}}$ is the local
	 system obtained by the orientation twist of $K=\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits\{\mathbb{G}\to GL(2,\mathbb{R})\}$. Now note that $K$
	 can also be identified with $\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits\{\mathfrak{G}_n\to D_{n+1}\}$ for any $n$ by Theorem
	 \ref{thm:crossed-groups}(b2). An automorphism of the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure $F_\Gamma$ (identical
	 on $\Gamma$) is therefore a section of a local system $\mathcal{L}$ on $\Gamma$ whose stalk at each
	 point is isomorphic to $K$. The final identification of $\mathcal{L}$ with $\underline K^{\operatorname{or}}$ and
	 of $q_*$ with the identity of  $\underline K^{\operatorname{or}}$ is left to the reader.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:segal} 
Let $\mathbf{C}$ be a combinatorial model category, and let $X \in \mathbf{C}_\Delta$ be a simplicial object.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item We say that $X$ is {\em 1-Segal} if, for every $n\geq 1$, the morphism
	\[
	f_n: X_n \longrightarrow (I[n], X)_R = X_1\times^R_{X_0} X_1 \times^R_{X_0} \cdots \times^R_{X_0} X_1,
	\]
	induced by the embedding $I[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta^n$, is a weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. 

	\item We say that $X$ is {\em 2-Segal} if, for every $n\geq 2$ and every triangulation $\mathcal{T}$ of $P_{n+1}$,
	the morphism
	\[
	f_\mathcal{T}: X_n \longrightarrow (\Delta^\mathcal{T}, X)_R,
	\]
	induced by the embedding $\Delta^\mathcal{T}\hookrightarrow \Delta^n$, is a weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. 

\end{enumerate}

A morphism $\varphi$ between ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ consists of a functor
	$\varphi: I(\Gamma) \to I(\Gamma')$ of incidence categories together with 
	a natural transformation $\eta: \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \circ \varphi \to
	\widetilde{I}_\Gamma$. We obtain a canonical sequence of morphisms
	\[
		\lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \longrightarrow 
		\lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \varphi \overset{\eta}{\longrightarrow}
		\lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma}
	\]
	whose composite defines the desired morphism ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma'} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$. Here the first
	morphism is the natural morphism $\lim F \to \lim F \varphi$ which exists for any
	functor $F: I(\Gamma') \to \mathbf{C}$ provided that both limits exist. It is straightforward to
	verify the functoriality of this association.

nodes.statement: To verify the 2-Segal property, we have to show that, for any subdivision of the n+1-gon P_n into two polygons P_m with vertices \0,1,dots, i, j, j+1, dots, n\ and P_l with vertices \i,i+1,dots, j\, the corresponding functor \[ f: Pi_1(D, \0,1,dots, i, j, j+1, dots, n\) coprod_Pi_1(D, \i,j\) Pi_1(D, \i,i+1,dots, j\) longrightarrow Pi_1(D,\0,1,dots,n\) \] is an isomorphism of groupoids. Up to isomorphism of groupoids we can alternatively describe f as the natural functor \[ f': Pi_1(P_m) coprod_Pi_1(P_1) Pi_1(P_l) longrightarrow Pi_1(P_n) \] induced from expressing P_n as the union of P_m and P_l with intersection P_m cap P_l = P_1. Here, all fundamental groupoids are taken with respect to the vertices of the respective polygon. The fact that f' is an isomorphism of groupoids is an easy instance of van Kampen's theorem (see, e.g., ). Similarly, to compute F(S,M), note that we can pass to the dual of a spanning graph in S setminus M to express (S,M) as a union of polygons. Interpreting formula in these terms, another application of van Kampen's theorem shows that F(S,M) is the fundamental groupoid Pi_1(S,M) computed as a colimit parametrized by the above polygonal subdivision of (S,M).

To verify the $2$-Segal property, we have to show that, for any subdivision of the $n+1$-gon $P_n$
into two polygons $P_m$ with vertices $\{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}$ and $P_l$ with vertices
$\{i,i+1,\dots, j\}$, the corresponding functor
\[
	f: \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}) \coprod_{\Pi_1(D, \{i,j\})} \Pi_1(D, \{i,i+1,\dots, j\}) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\})
\]
is an isomorphism of groupoids. Up to isomorphism of groupoids we can alternatively describe $f$
as the natural functor
\[
	f': \Pi_1(P_m) \coprod_{\Pi_1(P_1)} \Pi_1(P_l) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(P_n)
\]
induced from expressing $P_n$ as the union of $P_m$ and $P_l$ with intersection $P_m \cap P_l =
P_1$. Here, all fundamental groupoids are taken with respect to the vertices of the respective
polygon. The fact that $f'$ is an isomorphism of groupoids is an easy instance of van Kampen's theorem
(see, e.g., \cite[6.7.2]{brown}).
Similarly, to compute $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$, note that we can pass to the dual of a spanning graph in $S
\setminus M$ to express $(S,M)$ as a union of polygons. Interpreting formula \eqref{eq:statesum} in
these terms, another application of van Kampen's theorem shows that $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ is the fundamental
groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ computed as a colimit parametrized by the above polygonal subdivision of
$(S,M)$.

(a) Let $X$ be a space and $\mathcal{U} = (U_a)_{a\in V}$ be a locally finite covering of $X$
 by closed subspaces $U_a$. The {\em classical nerve}  of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex
 $\operatorname{N}\mathcal{U}=(V, \Sigma)$ where $\Sigma$ consists of finite $I\subset V$ s.t. $\bigcap_{v\in I} U_v\neq\emptyset$. 
  
  
  \vskip .2cm
  
  (b) In the situation (a), assume that the covering $\mathcal{U}$ is {\em saturated}, i.e., for any $U,U'\in \mathcal{U}$
  the intersection $U\cap U'$ is either empty or belongs to $\mathcal{U}$. The {\em monotone nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$
  is the simplicial complex
  $\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U} = (V.\Sigma^\leq)$, where $\Sigma^\leq$ consists of $I=\{v_0, \cdots, v_p\}\subset V$
  such that $U_{v_{s(0)}}\subset U_{v_{s(1)}} \subset \cdots\subset U_{v_{s(p)}}$ for some permutation
  $s$ of $\{0,1,\cdots, p\}$. Thus $|\operatorname{N}^\leq(\mathcal{U})|$ is the geometric realization of the simplicial
  set, given by the nerve of the poset of nonempty $U\in\mathcal{U}$.

nodes.name: \sl Proof:
nodes.statement: The construction and the argument of extend to the general case as follows. A point pin |A|-|A_infty| lies, by definition, strictly inside a simplex Delta^P for some tessellation P and thus is represented by the collection of its barycentric coordinates \[ (p_gamma)_gammainP, \,\, p_gamma > 0,\,\, sum p_gamma = 1, \] one for each arc gammainP. Consider a polygon (S'_i, M'_i) of P. To each edge e of S'_i we associate the ``length" p_e:=p_gamma where gamma is the arc of P that gave rise to e. Let l_e=sum_esubsetpartial S'_i p_e be the total ``length" of partial S'_i. Let S''_i be a disk in C with center 0 and circumference l_e. We can map M'_i bijectively to a subset M''_isubset partial S''_i so that the distances (on partial S''_i) between neighboring elements of M''_i match the corresponding numbers p_e for the edges of S'_i. In this way we get a stable marked Klein surface (S''_i, M''_i). We now glue the (S''_i, M''_i) together in the same fashion as the (S'_i, M'_i) are glued together to form (S, M). For this, we use the identifications of the boundary arcs of different S''_i which are affine linear in the standard angle (or arc length) coordinates on the circles partial S''_i. In this way we get a Klein surface (S'', M''), identified with (S,M) by a diffeomorphism unique up to isotopy. In other words, we get a point of Teich(S,M). This defines the map Psi_S,M. Its Mod(S,M)-equivariance is clear. The fact that Psi_S,M is a homeomorphism, was proved in in the oriented case. Suppose S is non-orientable, and let varpi: (widetilde S, widetilde M)to (S,M) be its orientation cover, with the deck involution tau preserving widetilde M. By equivariance, the homeomorphism \[ Psi_widetilde S, widetilde M: \,\, |A(widetilde S, widetilde M)|-|A_infty(widetilde S, widetilde M)| longrightarrow Teich (widetilde S, widetilde M) \] sends the involution tau_A: |A(widetilde S, widetilde M)|to |A(widetilde S, widetilde M)| induced by tau, to tau_Teich. Because of Proposition (b2), we are reduced to the following.
nodes.raw_latex:
The construction and the argument of \cite{harer}  extend to the general case as follows.
  A point $p\in |A|-|A_\infty|$ lies, by definition, strictly inside a simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ for some
  tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ and thus is represented by the collection of its barycentric coordinates
  \[
  (p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}, \,\, p_\gamma > 0,\,\, \sum p_\gamma = 1,
  \]
  one for each arc $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}$. 
  
  Consider a polygon $(S'_i, M'_i)$ of $\mathcal{P}$. To each edge $e$ of $S'_i$ we associate the ``length"
  $p_e:=p_\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is the arc of $\mathcal{P}$ that gave rise to $e$. Let $l_e=\sum_{e\subset\partial S'_i} p_e$
  be the total ``length" of $\partial S'_i$. 
  
  Let $S''_i$ be a disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with center $0$ and circumference $l_e$. We can map $M'_i$ bijectively
  to a subset $M''_i\subset \partial S''_i$ so that the distances (on $\partial S''_i$) between neighboring
  elements of $M''_i$ match the corresponding numbers $p_e$ for the edges of $S'_i$. In this way we
  get
  a stable marked Klein surface $(S''_i, M''_i)$. We now glue the $(S''_i, M''_i)$ together in the same
  fashion as the $(S'_i, M'_i)$ are glued together to form $(S, M)$. For this, we use the identifications
  of the boundary arcs of different $S''_i$ which are affine linear in the standard angle (or arc length)
  coordinates on the circles $\partial S''_i$. In this way we get a Klein surface $(S'', M'')$, identified with
  $(S,M)$ by a diffeomorphism unique up to isotopy. In other words, we get a point of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$.
  This defines the map $\Psi_{S,M}$. Its $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-equivariance is clear.
  
  The fact that $\Psi_{S,M}$ is a homeomorphism, was proved in \cite{harer} in the oriented case.
  Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, and let $\varpi: (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)\to (S,M)$
  be its orientation cover, with the deck involution $\tau$ preserving $\widetilde M$.
  By equivariance, the homeomorphism
  \[
  \Psi_{\widetilde S, \widetilde M}: \,\, |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)| 
  \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich} (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)
  \]
  sends  the involution $\tau_A: |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\to |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|$
  induced by $\tau$,  to $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$.
  Because of Proposition \ref{thm:klein-teich}(b2), we are reduced to the following.

nodes.name: \sl Proof of the lemma:
nodes.statement: A point pin |A(widetilde S, widetilde M)|^tau_A lies in a tau-invariant simplex Delta^widetildeP corresponding to a tau-invariant sub-tesselation widetildeP of (widetilde S, widetilde M). Let P be the set of arcs varpi(widetildegamma), widetildegammainwidetildeP. We claim that P is a sub-tesselation for (S,M). Indeed, the fact that widetilde gamma does not meet tau(widetilde gamma) (which both belong to widetildeP) means that varpi(widetildegamma) does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy between varpi(widetildegamma_1) and varpi(widetildegamma_2) implies that that widetilde gamma_2 is homotopic to either widetilde gamma_1 or to tau(widetilde gamma_1) (because varpi is an unramified covering). So P is a sub-tesselation.   arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}$. 
  We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not
  meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$
  does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy  between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and 
  $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either
  $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering).
  So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation.

  of $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. 
  Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation.

  p\,\,\in \,\,  \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A}

  of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates
  $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the

Let P be the set of arcs varpi(widetildegamma), widetildegammainwidetildeP. We claim that P is a sub-tesselation for (S,M). Indeed, the fact that widetilde gamma does not meet tau(widetilde gamma) (which both belong to widetildeP) means that varpi(widetildegamma) does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy between varpi(widetildegamma_1) and varpi(widetildegamma_2) implies that that widetilde gamma_2 is homotopic to either widetilde gamma_1 or to tau(widetilde gamma_1) (because varpi is an unramified covering). So P is a sub-tesselation. Further, suppose that widetildeP is a tessellation, Then any polygon (widetilde S'_i, widetilde M'_i) of widetildeP must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. Therefore P is a tessellation. We conclude that \[ p\,\,in \,\, bigl( |A(widetilde S, widetilde M)|-|A_infty(widetilde S, widetilde M)|bigr)^tau_A \] must lie in a simplex Delta^widetildeP where widetildeP=varpi^-1(P) is the preimage of a tessellation P of (S,M) and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates (p_widetildegamma)_widetildegammainwidetildeP which is tau-invariant. Such collections of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates (p_gamma)_gammainP, sum p_gamma=1, i.e., with points of the simplex Delta^P in |A(S,M)| - |A_infty(S,M)|. This proves the lemma and Theorem .
